text:
I. DIE MAASSE.

1. Vorwort.

Der Papyrus Ebers steht in der von uns hergestellten Publication¹) jedermann zur Verfügung. Wegen seiner durchaus correcten Schreibung hat er bisher die wichtigsten Dienste dem Grammatiker geleistet, der seiner nicht entrathen kann, sobald er sich der Erforschung des Alt-Aegyptischen im Gegensatz zu dem sogen. Neu-Aegyptischen der Papyri aus der XIX. und XX. Dynastie zuwendet. Für die Kulturgeschichte und die Geschichte der Medizin ist sein Inhalt gleichfalls von hohem Interesse und vielfach benutzt worden; der Arzt aber hat mit den vorgeschlagenen Mitteln bisher wenig zu machen gewusst, oder ist an den fragmentaren Übersetzungen einzelner Recepte vorübergegangen, schon weil von den verschriebenen Droguen viele unbestimmt bleiben mussten und über die Maasse, mit denen sie zu nehmen sind, gar nichts feststand. Auch die Absurditäten, welche der Pap. an einzelnen Stellen enthält, und die man mit weit grösserem Behagen als das Gute, wovon er voll ist, hervorzog, schreckten ihn ab. Da stellten wir uns denn die Aufgabe, diese schöne Handschrift so zu behandeln, dass sich auch Nichtaegyptologen, Ärzte, Naturkundige und Sprachforscher jeder Art ein zutreffendes Bild von ihr bilden können, und sie ist im Ganzen so beschaffen, dass sie ihrem Autor, wenn wir die Verhältnisse bedenken, unter denen er sie verfasste, zur Ehre gereicht.

1) Papyrus Ebers, conserviert in der Universitätsbibliothek zu Leipzig. Ein hieratisches Handbuch altaegyptischer Arzneikunde. Herausgegeben, mit Einleitung und der Übersetzung der vorkommenden Krankheiten versehen von Georg Ebers. Mit Unterstützung des kgl. sächs. Ministeriums des Kultus und öffentlichen Unterrichtes. Leipzig. W. Engelmann 1875.

translation:
I. THE MEASURES.

1. Preface.

The Ebers Papyrus is available to everyone through the publication we have produced.¹) On account of its thoroughly correct orthography, it has hitherto rendered the most important services to the grammarian, who cannot do without it as soon as he turns to the study of Old Egyptian as opposed to what is called New Egyptian in the papyri of the XIX. and XX. Dynasties. For cultural history and the history of medicine, its contents are likewise of great interest and have been widely used; however, the physician has hitherto known little what to make of the proposed remedies, or has passed over the fragmentary translations of individual recipes, not least because many of the prescribed drugs had to remain unidentified and nothing at all was established regarding the measures by which they were to be taken. The absurdities, too, which the papyrus contains at individual passages, and which people were far more inclined to bring forward than the good material of which it is full, deterred him. We therefore set ourselves the task of treating this fine manuscript in such a way that non-Egyptologists, physicians, naturalists, and philologists of every kind might form an accurate picture of it; and on the whole it is of such a nature that it does credit to its author, when we consider the circumstances under which he composed it.

1) Papyrus Ebers, preserved in the University Library at Leipzig. A hieratic handbook of ancient Egyptian medicine. Edited, with an introduction and translation of the diseases contained therein, by Georg Ebers. With the support of the Royal Saxon Ministry of Culture and Public Education. Leipzig. W. Engelmann 1875.

Wer mit anderen als den Hülfsmitteln unserer Specialwissenschaft die eigenen an unsere Forschungen zu knüpfen wünscht, der möge es an der Hand des hier zu Gebenden vertrauensvoll thun; denn wir folgen der Methode, kein Wort, das wir nicht mit aller Sicherheit verstehen, zu übertragen, den ganzen Text aber in consequenter Weise zu transscribieren und ihn mit einem eingehenden Commentar unter dem Texte zu versehen.

In solcher Weise denken wir später die ganze Handschrift zu behandeln, für's Erste aber unsere Methode nur auf einen der wichtigsten Abschnitte des Papyrus, den den Augenkrankheiten gewidmeten, auszudehnen.

Schon durch Herodot erfahren wir, dass das Specialistenwesen unter den aegyptischen Ärzten mit besonderer Strenge durchgeführt wurde. Der Oculist durfte nur die Leiden des Gesichtssinnes und keine anderen behandeln, und die Augenärzte vom Nil erfreuten sich unter den anderen Völkern des Alterthums des höchsten Ansehens. Aegypten ist auch heute noch eine bevorzugte Brut- und Beobachtungsstätte für Augenkrankheiten. Über diese und ihre Behandlungsweise von Seiten der Aegypter Näheres zu erfahren, liegt vielen unserer Oculisten am Herzen, und mehrere wandten sich denn auch mit Anfragen und der Aufforderung, ihnen das Verständniss des Papyrus zu eröffnen, an den Verfasser. So wählten wir das den Augenleiden gewidmete Kapitel, um unsere Methode an ihm zu erproben und den Ärzten, Linguisten und Freunden der Geschichte der Medizin eine sichere Unterlage für das eigene Studium zu bieten.

Über den Papyrus selbst, seine Herkunft, die Zeit seiner Entstehung etc. haben wir im Vorwort zu unserer Publication der Handschrift²) das Nöthige gesagt, und was zwischen dem Abschluss des genannten Werkes und dem heutigen Tage auf diesem Forschungsfelde geleistet wurde, das hat unsere fundamentalen Ansichten nur bestätigt und zu dem im Vorwort zum Pap. Ebers Bemerkten wenig Neues gefügt.

Unsere Handschrift ist das hermetische Buch über die Arzneimittel (περὶ φαρμάκων), das Clemens von Alexandria³) erwähnt, sie

Whoever wishes to connect their own work to our research using means other than the tools of our specialized discipline may do so with confidence, guided by what is offered here; for we follow the method of not transcribing any word we do not understand with complete certainty, but of transcribing the entire text in a consistent manner and providing it with a thorough commentary beneath the text.

In this way we intend later to treat the entire manuscript, but first to extend our method only to one of the most important sections of the papyrus — the one devoted to eye diseases.

Already through Herodotus we learn that specialization among Egyptian physicians was carried out with particular strictness. The oculist was permitted to treat only ailments of the sense of sight and no others, and the eye doctors of the Nile enjoyed the highest esteem among the other peoples of antiquity. Egypt is even today a favored breeding ground and place of observation for eye diseases. To learn more about these and their treatment by the Egyptians is a matter close to the hearts of many of our ophthalmologists, and several of them approached the author with inquiries and the request to open up the understanding of the papyrus to them. Thus we chose the chapter devoted to eye ailments in order to test our method on it and to offer physicians, linguists, and friends of the history of medicine a reliable foundation for their own study.

Regarding the papyrus itself, its origin, the time of its composition, etc., we have said what was necessary in the preface to our publication of the manuscript,²) and what has been accomplished in this field of research between the completion of that work and the present day has only confirmed our fundamental views and added little that is new to what was remarked in the preface to Pap. Ebers.

Our manuscript is the hermetic book on medicinal remedies (περὶ φαρμάκων) mentioned by Clement of Alexandria,³) it

Freilich wird die Transcription dadurch mit vielen Strichen belastet, deren Satz Unbequemlichkeiten verursacht; auch hat sie keine Annahme gefunden, und nach und nach sind die meisten Fachgenossen auch von der Londoner Methode abgewichen. Der lebhafteste Widerspruch erhob sich gegen die Umschrift derjenigen Zeichen, die man für Vocale ansah, und es ist in der That misslich, etliche von ihnen, denen ursprünglich sicher ein consonantischer Werth zukam, Vocale zu nennen. Dennoch empfiehlt es sich, bei unseren lateinischen Lettern zu bleiben, wenn man sich nicht — und auch dagegen spricht vieles — wie der unvergessliche Charas des koptischen Alphabetes bedienen will⁶); denn die Häkchen ị, ȝ, welche G. Steindorff in seiner vorzüglichen Dissertation zu gebrauchen vorschlug, bieten Schwierigkeiten, ergeben in ihrer Ver-

It was certainly written during the reign of the XVIII Dynasty, at the latest around 1500 B.C.; it is a compilation, in which very ancient⁴) and some foreign⁵) prescriptions were included, and the measurement signs, which appear alongside the names of the proposed medications, refer partly to volumetric measures and partly to weights.

2. The Transliteration.

The method of transliteration, which we employed in accordance with Prof. Dr. L. Stern in the preface to the publication, possessed certain advantages, in that it partly aligned with the system agreed upon at the Orientalist Congress in London (1874) in consultation with our advisory board, and partly made it possible to recognize whether the scribe employed alphabetic or syllabic signs. To be sure, the transcription is thereby burdened with many diacritical marks, whose typesetting causes inconveniences; moreover, it has not found acceptance, and gradually most colleagues have also departed from the London method. The liveliest objection arose against the transliteration of those signs that were regarded as vowels, and it is indeed problematic to call vowels those signs to which a consonantal value originally certainly belonged. Nevertheless, it is advisable to retain our Latin letters, if one does not wish — and there is much to be said against this as well — to use the unforgettable Charas of the Coptic alphabet⁶); for the hooks ị, ȝ, which G. Steindorff proposed using in his excellent dissertation, present difficulties, and yield in their application—

4) Pap. Ebers, LXVI, 15—18. A hair-growth remedy for the lady Šeš, mother of King Tâ.

5) LXIII, 8—11. A medicine for the eyes from a Semite from Kpnî, which is in any case a city of the Semitic land situated to the east of Egypt, and most likely means Byblos — Gebal.

6) With regard to the vowels, little would in any case be improved by this. In the choice especially of the so-called additional consonants, difficulties would often arise. In France, Maspero has in recent times departed considerably from the London method, particularly in the transcription of vowels. To be sure, he knows how to support his own system convincingly in various ways, but he might perhaps be willing to compromise, if another new system were on the verge of being generally adopted.

Es kommt ja bei der Transcription in erster Reihe darauf an, dass sie leicht und sicher erkennen lässt, welche Zeichen des Originals sie wiedergibt. In zweiter Linie soll sie, da sie nun einmal des Gebrauches von Strichen und Häkchen nicht zu entrathen vermag, dem Setzer möglichst geringe Schwierigkeiten bereiten und dem Auge nicht geradezu weh thun. Kommt sie diesen Anforderungen nach, wird sich auch das dritte Desiderium leicht erfüllen, dass sie annehmbar sei für möglichst viele Arbeiter und verständlich auch für andere als die aegyptologischen Forschungskreise.

Das Zeichen ⸗ᵃ vertritt, wie viele mit Hieroglyphen umschriebene semitische Namen lehren, das hebr. ע. Nichtorientalisten müssen gewarnt werden, das ‹ für den griechischen Spiritus asper, das › für den Spiritus lenis zu halten. mixed with Roman characters, creates an unpleasant sight for the typographer's eye, and beyond that they do not even render significantly better service than Roman letters furnished with appropriate diacritical marks for the transcription of certain sounds.⁷)

In transcription, the first priority is that it allow one to recognize easily and reliably which characters of the original it represents. In the second place, since it cannot avoid the use of dashes and hooks, it should cause the typesetter as little difficulty as possible and not be outright painful to the eye. If it meets these requirements, the third desideratum will also be easily fulfilled: that it be acceptable to as many scholars as possible and comprehensible to those outside Egyptological research circles as well.

The sign ⸗ᵃ represents, as many Semitic names transcribed with hieroglyphs teach us, the Hebrew ע. It is therefore by no means our "a" or any vowel at all; and yet I do not hesitate to transcribe it as a, since this indicates just as reliably as ‹ that the original is ⸗ᵃ, and moreover many Semitists transcribe ע as a. Non-Orientalists must be warned not to take the ‹ for the Greek spiritus asper and the › for the spiritus lenis. What matters most is a clear, unmistakable rendering of the base script; very little depends on the form of the signs, as long as they can be written and printed conveniently. Using the transcription to do justice to the history of individual sounds and to indicate the value they originally possessed is not feasible, or at least leads to an overloading that makes printing more difficult, more expensive, and more—

Erman, for use in the Zeitschrift für aegyptische Sprache und Alterthumskunde, combined the following transcription of the so-called vowels: 𓇋 i, ⸗ᵃ ı, 𓂝 i, 𓄿 y, 𓅱 w. We could sooner subscribe to this system, although 𓇋 and ⸗ᵃ do not at all suit us, and good reasons can be brought against 𓅱 == w, for which much can be said. Unfortunately, knowledge of this method came to us too late for us to make use of it in what follows. Later we may perhaps adopt it in general, but certainly in the transcription of consonants, since, for example, ḥ suits us better than χ for ☉, and d̠ appeals to us more than t for 𓌀.

ugly. Whoever nonetheless wishes to make such things comprehensible through transliteration, we would remind them that the Better is the enemy of the Good.

H. A. Erman also agreed in general with what has been said, in personal conversation with the author. We have attempted to do justice to his well-founded objections against 𓅓 = a, 𓇋𓇋 = ī and ꞷ = i, by transcribing 𓅓 = e, 𓇋𓇋 = y and ꞷ = ē. For 𓇋 we have kept a, although its original consonantal nature (j) is well known to us. For 𓂝 = d we have not decided lightly — for much speaks against it — but have nevertheless finally resolved to do so. For ⊙ = χ, ⟹ = ϑ, ⌐ = t we retain these for now, because we knew of nothing more convenient and more reliably available in every printing house to substitute for them.

Thus the simple and comprehensible transcription takes shape, which I employ following the London edition of 1874, after having subjected it to several emendations, as follows:

This method of transcription also has the advantage that it connects, where possible, to the familiar characters of Lepsius's standard alphabet that are available in printing houses. Not a single letter would need to be newly cast; for the ȧ, which is easily composed from a and ', is in any case for the trans-

schrift semitischer Texte in Gebrauch, das e mit den Puncta diareseos fehlt in keinem Setzerkasten, und wenn wir uns auch nicht hehlen, dass das griechische χ und ϑ, womit wir ☉ und ⟹ umschreiben, etwas Fremdes unter den übrigen römischen Lettern sind, so lassen wir sie doch unangetastet; denn wenn auch das ch und th dem Deutschen genügt, würden diese Buchstaben andere Sprachkreise zu einer Aussprache verleiten, die unseren von von der der Aegypter abweichen möchte. Anderwärts haben wir uns schon eingehend mit den Gründen beschäftigt, die uns hindern, ⟹ d zu umschreiben, und es bringt auch keinenfalls einen rein medialen Laut zum Ausdruck; doch fugten wir uns der von Erman warm empfohlenen und von mehreren Fachgenossen angenommenen Umschrift. Das t für ⌐ gibt im Druck ein nichts weniger als anmuthendes Bild, doch zogen wir es dem d vor, weil dies so gut wie das t ein conventionell gebildetes Zeichen ist und t sich durch das Standardalphabet und die Londoner Umschriftsmethode von 1874 in den Druckereien und unter den Fachgenossen einbürgerte. Seine wahre Aussprache wird sich dem englischen th genähert haben und einem solchen Laute gebührt als Unterlage eher ein t als ein d.

Für den Semitisten setzen wir neben die Lettern der Umschrift auch die ihnen entsprechenden des hebräischen Alphabetes. Den Consonanten gegenüber lässt sich dies mit einiger Sicherheit thun, da wir eine ziemlich grosse Anzahl von semitischen Namen und Lehnworten besitzen, die in hieroglyphischen Texten von den Aegyptern mit ihrem Alphabet umschrieben wurden und zu erkennen gestatten, welchen aegyptischen Lauten der Hierogrammat die semitischen gleichsetzte. Die Vocale bieten grössere Schwierigkeit, doch ist regelmässig ꜣ dem א entsprechend und \_\_ (freilich kein Vocal) dem ע. Für das ꜣꜣ tritt am häufigsten ' ein. ן und ☉ benutzte der Aegypter für die Umschrift des hebräischen ׳, und wir hätten es lieber mit w als u wiedergegeben, wenn uns nicht die Pluralenedungen und ähnliches bestimmten, bei dem alten u zu bleiben. Über das w ist viel gestritten worden. L. Stern und A. Erman widmeten ihm besondere Aufmerksamkeit, und ich glaube auf beider Zustimmung zählen zu dürfen, wenn ich es e umschreibe.

140 Georg Ebers. [8

script of Semitic texts is in use; the e with the puncta diareseos is absent from no typesetter's case, and even if we do not conceal from ourselves that the Greek χ and ϑ, with which we transcribe ☉ and ⟹, are somewhat foreign among the other Roman letters, we nonetheless leave them untouched; for even though ch and th suffice for Germans, these letters would lead other language communities to a pronunciation that might deviate from ours and from that of the Egyptians. Elsewhere we have already dealt extensively with the reasons that prevent us from transcribing ⟹ as d, and it does not by any means express a purely medial sound; yet we submitted to the transcription warmly recommended by Erman and adopted by several colleagues. The t for ⌐ produces in print an image that is anything but attractive, yet we preferred it to d, because the latter is just as much a conventionally formed sign as t, and t became established in printshops and among specialists through the standard alphabet and the London transcription method of 1874. Its true pronunciation will have been close to the English th, and for such a sound a t is a more appropriate basis than a d.

For the Semitist, we place beside the letters of the transcription the corresponding letters of the Hebrew alphabet. With regard to the consonants this can be done with some confidence, since we possess a fairly large number of Semitic names and loanwords that were transcribed by the Egyptians in hieroglyphic texts using their alphabet, and which allow us to recognize which Egyptian sounds the hierogrammist equated with the Semitic ones. The vowels present greater difficulty, yet ꜣ regularly corresponds to א and \_\_ (which is of course not a vowel) to ע. For ꜣꜣ the sign ' most frequently appears. ן and ☉ were used by the Egyptians to transcribe the Hebrew ׳, and we would have preferred to render it as w rather than u, had not the plural endings and similar considerations determined us to retain the old u. Much has been disputed about the w. L. Stern and A. Erman devoted particular attention to it, and I believe I may count on the agreement of both when I transcribe it as e.

3. The Determinative Signs.

Whoever has familiarized himself with our transcription alphabet will be able to grasp easily and precisely the phonetic value of any text rendered with its help; yet hieroglyphic writing also offers an explanatory and illustrative element that makes it easier to determine the meaning of many words, especially those denoting concrete objects. We refer to the so-called determinative signs. These are placed after the phonetically written word and indicate to which conceptual category it belongs. Names belonging to the plant kingdom are determined with ꜥꜣ, or, if they denote trees, with () or ⊕. After the names of drinks and liquids appears the image of a hollow vessel ©, ⊕ or ∞, and after those of quadrupeds a piece of their hide with the tail ꜣ.

It is easy to understand what great and welcome assistance these signs provide precisely for determining the conceptual value of words that denote remedies or body parts proposed for treatment. We therefore consider it necessary to make these important aids accessible to non-Egyptologists as well, and for this reason we place after the name of each medicament its determinative.

After this, one must examine which measures are to be regarded as measures of volume, which as measures of weight, and only then will one be able to establish the weight or content of the individual measures and the value of the fractional signs, which prescribe taking so and so many parts of a unit. Finally, the prescriptions of the entire papyrus must again be examined, in order to test the correctness of the results obtained and to decide whether certain signs and numbers in a particular position might mean something special.

2. The Specific Measures of the Papyrus.

There are four measures which the Egyptian physician uses most frequently. For all weighings, one and the same unit is used everywhere and without exception. It breaks down into fractions which we shall have to examine more closely, yet the name of this so extensively used apothecary weight is mentioned nowhere. Among the measures of volume there are 3 which are to be regarded as properly calibrated measures, and of these only two are subdivided into parts. The most frequently occurring is the measure written hieratically as ꞁ, which probably corresponds to the hieroglyphic dnat ꞓ and with which ordinarily only liquid substances are measured, as well as the apothecary measure ꞓ Re or Ro, which is mentioned at no point in the papyrus, but which seems to us certainly and indeed quite frequently to be intended. Parts of these two volume measures are also prescribed, while the third is ordered only in full quantities²⁴). It is called hnu ȿ, hnu ȿ, hn (hin), corresponds in name to the Hebrew הִין and is not to be distinguished from the hnu that appears alongside it. The unit of weight, as we firmly believe, is correctly calculated by Hultsch at 6.06⅔ grams; 1/16 of this would represent only a fraction of a berry, as we found from weighing grapes that we had prepared for us at the Schellenberg pharmacy in Wiesbaden by the obliging gentlemen provisors. It is, however, difficult to believe that a small piece of grape was added to the medicament. On the contrary, these prescriptions are best explained if we connect špt ☉ (the Coptic ϭⲉⲙ means only "to shear") with the ancient Egyptian root šp, which denotes giving off a liquid, spitting it out and pouring it. H. Brugsch rightly derives from the same root the word šp, used in our papyrus for "blind," špu or šup, which originally means having run out, dripped from the eye. Our špt ☉ must therefore — and the determinative does not contradict this — be understood as the droplet-like discharge of the grape and the gum tree. We therefore translate šept nt ʽerr as grape juice, špt ☉ nt qnyt as gum drops, and we will have hit upon the correct meaning.

The term prt designates the metallic grains of stibium or antimony and the resinous grains of frankincense. 26 different kinds of prt, which belong almost entirely to the plant or mineral kingdom, are prescribed.

18. We do not enumerate the cakes and types of bread with which the drugs are to be mixed or into which the medications are to be shaped, although these also relate to the form of the prescribed remedies. XI, 1 and 2, for example, require that the proposed substances be made into a šns bread and eaten. XLVII, 4 includes a hât flatbread of the same bread type among the medications. The ordinary bread is proposed as a medicament, to be weighed and measured.

Extraordinarily varied are the vessels that were used in the Egyptian pharmacy, and this certainly attests to the refined development of pharmacy in ancient Egypt. Among them belong, as mentioned, the measures of capacity already noted above: the Hin and the dnât.

19. The Hin or Ḥnu. LXV, 14 states that the medication is to be placed in a hnu (Hin-jug); a new Hin-jug is mentioned several times; LXXX, 16 states that the remedy is to be placed in a new Hin-jug; XLIX, 20 states that the woman etc. is to drink the remedy from a Hnu-jug; indeed, the material of the jug itself is proposed as a medicament: LXIII, 8 and XCIV, 12. From this it follows that the words Hin or Ḥnu are also used to designate a specifically shaped vessel without reference to its contents, just as we call a glass holding more or less than 0.5 liters a "Seidel" on account of its shape, and use the words "Tonne" and "Fass" sometimes to denote a specific measure and weight, and sometimes merely a wooden vessel made by a cooper.

20. How the dnât vessel relates to this matter we shall examine further below. XXXIV, 5 and 6 states that a dnât vessel filled with water is to be set out overnight; however, by this may be meant, as we intend to show, either a calibrated or an uncalibrated vessel.

a. Stückweis zu Nehmendes und seine Anzahl.

Begeben wir uns nun an die Bestimmung der Maasse, nach denen die verordneten Medicamente theils gewogen theils gemessen werden sollen, so haben wir gerade hier der Methode zu gedenken, die streng untersagt, aus einzelnen Angaben Schlüsse zu ziehen, während sie gebieterisch fordert, in jedem einzelnen Falle die ganze Handschrift im Auge zu behalten und diese — gerade mit Rücksicht auf die Maasse — sich durch sich selbst erklären zu lassen.

These words indicating quantities or meaning containers designate collectively the doses or vessels of metal, clay, stone, wood or cloth to be used in the dispensary, which were not calibrated and may not be regarded as measures of a definite capacity. A rhdt ß is a kettle, a zeu ß a pot or jug, whose size could vary as much as our vessels with the same name; indeed, under 19 and 20 we showed that even the calibrated measures Hin, hnu and dnat are not always mentioned in the sense of specific measures, but probably only with regard to their form, as vessels in general.

4. Definite Weights and Hollow Measures.

a. Items to be taken by the piece and their number.

If we now turn to the determination of the measures by which the prescribed medicaments are to be partly weighed and partly measured, we must here recall the method which strictly forbids drawing conclusions from individual statements, while it imperiously demands that in each individual case the entire manuscript be kept in view and allowed — with particular regard to the measures — to explain itself by itself.

The medicaments are to be measured or weighed, unless in individual cases a specific number of the proposed object, or a part of it other than a measured portion, is prescribed. bringen soll, verordnet dem leidenden Kleinen mit einem in Öl gesottenen alten Buche (Papyrusrolle) den Leib zu bestreichen, etc. Diese Dinge, die nicht eigentlich zu den Maassen gehören, erklären sich von selbst.

§. b. Die Wägung.

Hat man sämmtliche Recepte zu Rathe gezogen, so lässt sich das mit dem Hohlmaass zu Messende leicht von dem zu Wägenden unterscheiden, obgleich die Gewichtseinheit und eines der am häufigsten gebrauchten Hohlmaasse nie bei Namen genannt werden.

Man bedient sich für alles zu Wägende nur eines Gewichtes, dessen Einheit nicht genannt wird; seine Theilung erfolgt aber überall nach dem gleichen System. In der Einleitung zum Pap. Ebers S. 48 schlugen wir vor, dies Medicinalgewicht mit dem späteren arabischen Dirhem oder der Drachme in Verbindung zu bringen und die Einheit, deren sich der Verfasser des Papyrus bediente, der Doppeldrachme gleichzusetzen, die etwa 6,220 Gramm wog. Spätere Studien brachten uns von dieser Ansicht ab, und es will uns sicher erscheinen, dass wir in der erwähnten Einheit ein Gewicht zu erkennen haben, welches mit dem System des [hieroglyph] udn [hieroglyph] oder [hieroglyph] udn zusammenhing, wie P. Bortolotti³⁵) scharfsinnig nachwies, dem Kubus der kleineren Elle an Gewicht gleichkommen sollte. Dies sehen wir überall benutzen, wo es edele Metalle zu wägen gilt; und daneben das [hieroglyph] qt, welches dem koptischen ϪΤ die Drachme sprachlich entspricht und den zehnten Theil eines udn [hieroglyph] wog. Doch dies Qt [hieroglyph] 9,096 Gramm wäre zu schwer als dass wir es für die Einheit unseres Papyrus halten dürften, und so stimmen wir Hultsch bei³⁶), wenn er ²/₃ des Qt für diese Einheit erklärt, welche dann 6,064 Gramm betragen hätte, ein Gewicht, das nicht zu weit von unserer ersten Bestimmung³⁷) abweicht, nach der es 6,220 Gramm gewogen haben würde.

is intended to bring relief, prescribing that the suffering child be rubbed on the body with an old book (papyrus roll) boiled in oil, etc. These things, which do not strictly belong to the subject of measures, are self-explanatory.

§. b. Weighing.

Once all the prescriptions have been consulted, it is easy to distinguish what is to be measured by volume from what is to be weighed, even though the unit of weight and one of the most frequently used volumetric measures are never mentioned by name.

For everything to be weighed, only one weight is used, whose unit is not named; its subdivision, however, follows the same system throughout. In the introduction to Pap. Ebers, p. 48, we proposed to connect this medicinal weight with the later Arabic dirhem or the drachma, and to equate the unit used by the author of the papyrus with the double drachma, which weighed approximately 6.220 grams. Later studies led us away from this view, and it now seems certain to us that in the unit in question we should recognize a weight which was connected with the system of [hieroglyph] udn [hieroglyph] or [hieroglyph] udn, as P. Bortolotti³⁵) cleverly demonstrated, and which was meant to equal in weight the cube of the smaller cubit. We see this used everywhere when precious metals are to be weighed; and alongside it the [hieroglyph] qt, which linguistically corresponds to the Coptic ϪΤ as the drachma and weighed one tenth of a udn [hieroglyph]. But this Qt [hieroglyph] of 9.096 grams would be too heavy for us to accept as the unit of our papyrus, and so we agree with Hultsch³⁶) when he identifies ²/₃ of the Qt as this unit, which would then have amounted to 6.064 grams, a weight not too far removed from our first determination³⁷), according to which it would have weighed 6.220 grams.

As for the subdivision of this unnamed unit of 6.064 grams, which we nevertheless, for the sake of convenience, call "drachma" —

a. Das Hin.

Von den Hohlmaassen werden zwei bei Namen genannt. Erstens das Hin, dem wir das Ḥnụ ẖ gleichstellen und zweitens das dnat, welches hieratisch 7 geschrieben wird und hieroglyphisch 𓎆.

160 Georg Ebers. [28

to continue what is meant, it remains as stated in the introduction to the Pap. Ebers; for it does indeed break down into fractions whose numerators are 1 and whose denominators are powers of 2. Thus from our unit of weight no other parts are taken than ½, ¼, ⅛, 1/16, 1/32, and 1/64. The unit was divided into 64 or respectively 128 parts. This method of calculation, in which no fractions other than those with numerator 1 are used, is genuinely Egyptian and was also adopted by the learned Greeks at Alexandria; for so significant a physicist and mechanician as Hero made use of it, and despite its clumsiness it remained in use until the Middle Ages.³⁸)

Where we thus see alongside prescribed drugs ¼, ⅛, 1/32, and 1/64, these refer to parts of the unit of weight of 6.064 grams, which we call the drachma. ½ is ordinarily to be understood as a liquid measure. After careful consideration of all the quantity specifications contained in the papyrus, the rule can be established that wherever we find a fraction after the name of a drug whose denominator is a power of 2, the ingredient is to be weighed, while by contrast medicaments with fractions belonging to a different system of division, such as ⅓, ½ ½ = ⅚, etc., are to be measured by liquid volume.

Very many medicaments are composed of a greater or lesser number of drugs. After each stands the |, and they are therefore to be taken in equal parts. Whether here the unit is to be understood as a weight or a liquid measure, we shall have to examine further below.

b, c. The Liquid Measures.

a. The Hin.

Of the liquid measures, two are mentioned by name. First, the Hin, which we equate with the Ḥnụ ẖ, and second the dnat, which is written in hieratic as 7 and hieroglyphically as 𓎆.

The Hin, "the measuring vessel par excellence," as Hultsch expresses it, is a handleless jug ẖ, which at the top has such a strongly projecting—

tretenden Rand haben musste, dass man LXIII, 18 den Rand³⁹) eines neuen Hingefässes als Medicament verordnen konnte. Auch die Scherbe eines solchen wird zerrieben und mit erwärmtem Öl XCIV, 12 als Heilmittel vorgeschrieben. Den Rand brachte man an dem Gefässe an, um den Ausguss aus demselben bequemer zu bewirken. Das Zeichen, mit dem das Wort hin ᵹ determiniert wird, gibt einen Begriff von dem Aussehen dieses Maasses. Da sich nun etliche altaegyptische Krüge erhalten haben, auf denen verzeichnet steht wie viele Hin sie fassten (9 Hin, 11 Hin, 21 Hin, 40 Hin etc.), konnte Chabas die Bestimmung des Inhaltes eines Hin mit Glück unternehmen. Obgleich man nun berücksichtigen muss, dass bei der Nachmessung von Gefässen aus dem Alterthum das immer abgezogen werden muss, was Chabas den Raum „de non remplissage" nennt, lässt sich das Hin doch auf 0,456 Liter bestimmen. Diesen Ansatz hat Hultsch, der gründlichste und scharfsinnigste Kenner auf dem Gebiet des Messwesens der Alten, welcher die Vorarbeiten der Aegyptologen (Chabas, Dumichen, Eisenlohr etc.) nachprüfte, bestätigt, und wir schliessen uns ihm willig an, da es uns leider versagt ist, die Museen nach neuen gezeichneten Hingefässen zu durchsuchen und wir sicher sind, dass, sollten auch noch mehrere entdeckt werden, sich höchstens an der dritten Decimalstelle eine Änderung empfehlen würde.

Bemerkt sei, dass das aegyptische mit dem hebräischen Hin nichts gemein hat als den Namen; denn solches enthielt 42 Log und der Inhalt des aegyptischen Hin kam dem von einem einzigen Log und daneben auch dem eines babylonischen Sechzigstel nahe. So fasste das hebräische etwa 12 mal so viel als das aegyptische Hin von 0,456 Liter. Wo es im Papyrus gebraucht werden soll, wird es im Ganzen zu nehmen verordnet. Ein Bruchtheil des Hin kommt nicht vor; nur kann in unten zu erwähnenden Fällen bisweilen ½ darauf bezogen werden. Einmal, LXXXV, 15 und 16, sollen 6 Hin 4 Tage lang eingenommen und LIV, 18 soll 1 Hin 6 mal 4 Tage lang getrunken werden, sonst wird im ganzen Papyrus nie mehr als 1 Hin zu brauchen verordnet und was damit gemessen werden soll, sind theils flüssige Substanzen wie Wasser, Wein, Milch und Honig, theils feste wie Korn und Datteln in verschiedener Zubereitung.

translation:
99] Pap. Ebers. Measures and the Chapter on Eye Diseases. 161

the projecting rim had to be such that in LXIII, 18 the rim³⁹) of a new hin-vessel could be prescribed as a medicine. The shard of such a vessel is also ground up and prescribed as a remedy mixed with warmed oil at XCIV, 12. The rim was attached to the vessel in order to make pouring from it more convenient. The sign by which the word hin ᵹ is determined gives an idea of the appearance of this measure. Since a number of ancient Egyptian jugs have been preserved, on which is recorded how many hin they held (9 hin, 11 hin, 21 hin, 40 hin, etc.), Chabas was able successfully to undertake the determination of the capacity of a hin. Although one must take into account that when remeasuring ancient vessels, one must always subtract what Chabas calls the "de non remplissage" space, the hin can nonetheless be determined at 0.456 liters. This estimate has been confirmed by Hultsch, the most thorough and acute authority in the field of ancient metrology, who checked the preliminary work of the Egyptologists (Chabas, Dümichen, Eisenlohr, etc.), and we readily concur with him, since we are unfortunately unable to search the museums for newly identified hin-vessels, and we are confident that even if more were discovered, a change would be warranted at most in the third decimal place.

It should be noted that the Egyptian hin has nothing in common with the Hebrew hin except the name; for the latter contained 42 log, and the capacity of the Egyptian hin was close to that of a single log and also close to a Babylonian sixtieth. Thus the Hebrew hin held about 12 times as much as the Egyptian hin of 0.456 liters. Wherever it is to be used in the Papyrus, it is prescribed to be taken as a whole. A fraction of the hin does not occur; only in cases to be mentioned below is ½ of it sometimes referred to. Once, at LXXXV, 15 and 16, 6 hin are to be taken over 4 days, and at LIV, 18, 1 hin is to be drunk 6 times over 4 days; otherwise, never more than 1 hin is prescribed for use anywhere in the Papyrus, and what is to be measured with it consists partly of liquid substances such as water, wine, milk and honey, and partly of solid items such as grain and dates in various preparations.

39) Literally "the lips," which, as in Hebrew, is also used to mean the bank or shore of rivers.

4, c. β. Das Dnât 7.

Der Inhalt des dnât 7 = ℌ ist schwerer bestimmbar. Im Decret von Kanopus (Tafel von Tanis 2/3) entspricht dem aegyptischen dnât ⊏ das griechische xανοῦν (κάνεον), das einen Korb (canistrum), aber auch ein irdenes Gefäss bedeutet. Sein kopt. Äquivalent ⲍⲁⲛⲟ (⊏ = ⲭ?) wird nicht nur benutzt, um einen Korb, sondern auch um eine Kiste zu bezeichnen. In hierogyl. Texten wird das Wort dnâ, dnâ-t ℌ auch begleitet von ⌀, das gewöhnlich Wein- oder Ölgefässe determiniert, oder dem Maassenzeichen für Metalle ℙ, woraus hervorgeht, dass es auch metallene dnâtgefässe gab. Brugsch (Wörterb. II, S. 1369) fand auch zu Karnak über dem Bilde einer flachen Schüssel das Wort dnâ. Im Text des Pap. Harris I, 28, 12 wird unsere Gruppe dnât ℌ, zu Karnak und auf der Tafel von Kanop. nur dnâ, demot. dnu geschrieben, und so haben wir denn dnâ und dnât sicher für das gleiche Wort zu halten. Dass der Wurzel dn, dnâ die Bedeutung von theilen innewohnt, ist längst bekannt. Gewiss bedeutet auch das alte dn ⌀ und âdn ⌀ hören, lauschen ursprünglich die Worte der Rede sondern oder zertheilen (mit dem Ohre), ganz ähnlich wie âd ⌀ lesen als das Sondern, Zertheilen der Rede (mit dem Munde) gefasst ward. Dennoch bezeichnet das ℌ weder in unserem Papyrus noch sonst einen unbestimmten Theil, etwa eine Portion. Wohl benutzt es der Arzt, der unsere Handschrift verfasste, um von einem dnâ ℌ gefässe mit Rücksicht auf die Form und nicht auf den Inhalt zu reden, sonst aber haben wir darin stets ein Maass zu erkennen, aber welches? translation:
162 Georg Ebers. [30

4, c. β. The Dnât 7.

The content of the dnât 7 = ℌ is more difficult to determine. In the Decree of Canopus (Tanis tablet 2/3), the Egyptian dnât ⊏ corresponds to the Greek κανοῦν (κάνεον), which means a basket (canistrum), but also an earthen vessel. Its Coptic equivalent ⲍⲁⲛⲟ (⊏ = ⲭ?) is used not only to designate a basket, but also a chest. In hieroglyphic texts, the word dnâ, dnâ-t ℌ is also accompanied by ⌀, which ordinarily determines wine or oil vessels, or by the measure sign for metals ℙ, from which it follows that there were also metallic dnât-vessels. Brugsch (Dictionary II, p. 1369) also found at Karnak, above the image of a flat bowl, the word dnâ. In the text of Pap. Harris I, 28, 12, our group dnât ℌ is written at Karnak and on the Canopus tablet simply as dnâ, in Demotic as dnu, and so we must certainly regard dnâ and dnât as the same word. That the root dn, dnâ carries the meaning of dividing has long been known. Certainly the old dn ⌀ and âdn ⌀, meaning to hear, to listen, originally expressed the separating or dividing of the words of speech (with the ear), quite similarly to how âd ⌀, to read, was understood as the separating, dividing of speech (with the mouth). Nevertheless, the ℌ designates in our papyrus, as elsewhere, neither an indefinite part nor a portion. The physician who composed our manuscript uses it to speak of a dnâ ℌ vessel with reference to its form and not to its content; otherwise we must always recognize in it a measure — but which one? The determination is difficult; for whether we, in transcribing this 7 as dnât, have hit upon the right reading is probable, yet by no means certain, since it does not appear written out anywhere in the entire manuscript. Let us then examine with what value a measure 7 and ℌ otherwise occurs.

First, as Dümichen⁴⁰) showed from calculations in the calendar of Medinet Habu, the ℌ, which we equate with the 7 here,

31) Pap. Ebers. The Measures and the Chapter on Eye Diseases. 163

half of the ápt or Epha, which amounts to 20 Hin or (according to Hultsch's⁴⁴ precise calculation) 9.11 liters; the ḥt, which in Med. Habu alternates with ○ and ⊕○ and is read by Dümichen l. l. as ḥotep, cannot be considered here; for it encompasses 160 Hin or 72.90 liters, for which Hultsch refines Dümichen's 73 liters 60 centiliters. That a measure storable in a barrel would be inapplicable for prescriptions in which a unit of weight of 6.06⅘ grams was sometimes to be divided into 64 parts is self-evident; indeed, even 9.11 liters, which are often prescribed in whole amounts and never in fractions smaller than ⅓, can certainly not be conceived as an additive to such tiny doses as one sixty-fourth of 6.06⅘, i.e., 0.09⅘ grams. That would have produced a dilution which would have nullified the effect of the simple drugs prescribed, and what patients were otherwise expected to take proves clearly enough that Egyptian physicians were worlds apart from homeopathic principles. Where ⅓ or ¾ were to be taken, it could only ever refer to a hollow measure, and specifically to one whose division belonged to the sexagesimal system, such as the sixtieth part of the artabe (0.608 liters), which we called dnât. When Stern, who otherwise did not go into greater detail about the measures of our papyrus, also regarded fractions belonging to the weight system as parts of the 7, we believe he was mistaken. The X means, as we shall see, ¼, and as such it cannot ordinarily refer to the 7 belonging to the sexagesimal system. One does also find ⌐7 and +7, i.e. ½ dnât and ⅓ dnât, but never ×7 = ¼ dnât or 7̄7̄7̄7 7 = ⅛ dnât.

Now mention must also be made of another 7, which one might be inclined at first glance to take for the hollow measure used alongside the Hin, divided into parts, and that is the 7 of the mathematical Papyrus Rhind, which Eisenlohr⁴⁸) correctly explains as ⅞ of the Hin or 20 Ro, and which therefore, since the Hin measures 0.456 liters, would hold 0.255 liters. This measure alone must not be overlooked, since it belongs to the system of the great ḥḳe hollow measure, of which the Ro occurs as the 320th part and into which 10 Hin go. Since this Ro, as we shall see, is an Egyptian apothecary measure that was also adopted into the practice of other peoples, and which we also find in Pap. Ebers, it is tempting to equate the 7 of the mathematical Pap. Rhind, which contains 20 Ro, with the same sign in our manuscript. Nevertheless, this does not work; firstly because several recipes contradict it, demanding for the whole dnât a greater capacity than the 0.285 liters that correspond to the 7 of the math. Pap. Ein einziger Satz in dieser Handschrift scheint zu empfehlen, das ⌐ für weit grösser zu halten nicht nur als das ⌐ des math. Pap. Rhind, das nur ¼ des Hin = 0,285 Liter fasst, sondern auch als das oben für 1⁄60 der Artabe erklärte ⌐ des Pap. Ebers, welches 0,608 Liter, also noch nicht 1½ Hin enthalten würde. Diese Stelle, Pap. Ebers XXXIV, 5 und 6, lautet: [hieroglyphic text]
Fass meine Hand, Greif meine Hand ⌐ kraut. Hinzusetzen (in) einem ⌐ dnât Wasser die Nacht hindurch und zu trinken ein bnugefäss des Wassers, das darin ist, 4 Tage lang. Diese Verordnung kann also so gefasst werden, als solle aus einem ⌐ dnât 4 Tage hintereinander je 1 bnu ß oder Hin Wasser getrunken werden. Hieraus könnte man schliessen, dass das dnât ⌐ gefäss mindestens 4 Hin ß oder Hin und also statt 0,608 wenigstens 1,824 Liter (4 × 1 Hin zu 0,456 Liter) fassen müsste. Doch diese Verordnung braucht uns nicht irre zu machen, denn S. 150 (18) unter 20 ward schon gezeigt, dass das Wort Hin und bnu ß nicht nur gebraucht ward, um ein Gefäss von genau bestimmter Mächtigkeit, sondern auch — nur mit Rücksicht auf die Form des Gefässes — einen Krug im Allgemeinen ohne Rücksicht auf seine Grösse zu bezeichnen. Das Gleiche scheint auch für das dnât-Gefäss gegolten zu haben, und es ist dabei zu bedenken, dass an unserer Stelle nicht nur Wasser, sondern auch von der seltsam benannten Pflanze »Fass meine Hand, greif meine Hand« eine nicht nach dem Maass bestimmte, also beliebige Menge in das Gefäss gethan werden sollte. Zwischen [hieroglyph] str hinstellen und ⌐ das dnât ist die Präposition [hieroglyph] zu ergänzen, und diese kann ebensowohl »mit« als »in« übertragen werden. Soll nun ein Kraut in einem ⌐ dnât Wasser die Nacht hindurch hingestellt werden — jedenfalls um das Wasser mit dem Pflanzensaft zu durchdringen — so ist das ⌐ gar nicht als Gefäss, sondern als Maass zu fassen, und das

35] Pap. Ebers. The Measures and the Chapter on Eye Diseases. 167

Ro add, having nothing to do with the sexagesimal system and breaking down only into fractions with numerator 1 whose denominators are divisible only by 2, while into the fractions of the ⌐ of Pap. Ebers the 3 goes evenly.

A single passage in this manuscript seems to recommend considering the ⌐ as far larger not only than the ⌐ of the mathematical Pap. Rhind, which holds only ¼ of the Hin = 0.285 liters, but also larger than the ⌐ of Pap. Ebers explained above as 1⁄60 of the Artabe, which would contain 0.608 liters, thus still not 1½ Hin. This passage, Pap. Ebers XXXIV, 5 and 6, reads: [hieroglyphic text]
"Grasp my hand, seize my hand" ⌐ herb. To place (in) a ⌐ dnât of water overnight and to drink one bnu-vessel of the water that is in it, for 4 days. This prescription can therefore be understood as meaning that from one ⌐ dnât, 4 days in succession, one bnu ß or Hin of water is to be drunk each time. From this one might conclude that the dnât ⌐ vessel would have to hold at least 4 Hin ß or Hin, and thus instead of 0.608 liters, at least 1.824 liters (4 × 1 Hin at 0.456 liters). Yet this prescription need not mislead us, for on p. 150 (18) under 20 it was already shown that the word Hin and bnu ß was used not only to designate a vessel of precisely determined capacity, but also — with regard only to the shape of the vessel — a jug in general without reference to its size. The same seems to have applied to the dnât-vessel as well, and it is to be borne in mind that at our passage not only water but also an unspecified, arbitrary quantity of the oddly named plant "Grasp my hand, seize my hand" was to be placed into the vessel. Between [hieroglyph] str placing and ⌐ the dnât, the preposition [hieroglyph] is to be supplied, and this can be rendered as either "with" or "in." If a herb is now to be placed in a ⌐ dnât of water overnight — presumably to infuse the water with the plant's juice — then the ⌐ is not to be understood as a vessel at all, but as a measure, and the

Das bleibt stehen, dass 4 ḥnu von einem Medicament genommen werden sollen, zu dem nur 1 dnât 7 Wasser gehörte, doch mag das Kraut, mit dem jenes während der Nacht zu stehen hatte, viel Platz genommen haben und mit in den ḥnukrug zu schöpfen gewesen sein. Hätt' es sich aber auch nur um die vom Saft des Krautes imprägnierte Flüssigkeit gehandelt, so brauchte uns die angeführte Stelle schon darum nicht in unserer Bestimmung des 7 irre zu machen, weil das ḥnu ƍ, wie gesagt, auch gebraucht ward, um einen bestimmt geformten Krug von beliebiger Grösse zu bezeichnen und sich in dieser Verbindung (auch die Pflanze soll weder gewogen noch gemessen werden) von dem dnât 7 dasselbe annehmen lässt. Zum Schluss sei nochmals hervorgehoben, dass diese verschieden zu deutende Stelle die einzige ist, welche Bedenken gegen unsere Bestimmung erwecken könnte, während alle anderen für die Richtigkeit derselben sprechen.

4, c. γ. Das Ro.

Das Maass Ro ist uns bereits als kleinster Theil des in 320 Theile zerlegten bše des math. Pap. Rhind begegnet und wir haben bemerkt, dass es, obzwar es dort nie genannt wird, auch in unserem Papyrus vorkommt. Dies werden wir nunmehr zu begründen haben. Seine, des Ro Verwendung in dem die Heilmittel der aegyptischen Medizin zusammenfassenden hermetischen Buche — denn das ist der Pap. Ebers — war von vorn herein zu erwarten. Die Receptkunde der Aegypter, für deren feine Ausbildung unsere Handschrift ein so glänzendes Zeugniss ablegt, ist nämlich nicht Alleingut der am Nil thätigen Ärzte geblieben; vielmehr ward sie ihnen von gelehrten griechischen Medizinern in Alexandrien abgesehen und in die Arzneiwissenschaft der Hellenen übertragen. Ist es nun auch noch nicht gar lange
translation:
168 Georg Ebers, [36

The later ám means equally "from it" as well as "out of it." It is therefore probable that in our sentence no specific vessel is meant, from which one is to drink 4 ḥnu ƍ each day for 4 days, and we may translate: Take my hand, grasp my herb (in any quantity) to be added (in any vessel) with one dnât 7 of water overnight, and to drink 4 ḥnu ƍ of the resulting liquid, every day for 4 consecutive days. It remains the case that 4 ḥnu of a medicine is to be taken, to which only 1 dnât 7 of water belonged; yet the herb with which it had to stand overnight may have taken up a great deal of space and may have needed to be scooped into the ḥnu-jug along with it. But even if it had only been a matter of the liquid impregnated by the juice of the herb, the passage cited would not for that reason alone need to mislead us in our determination of 7, since the ḥnu ƍ, as stated, was also used to denote a specifically shaped jug of any size, and in this connection (the plant also being neither weighed nor measured) the same may be assumed from the dnât 7. In conclusion, let it once again be emphasized that this variously interpretable passage is the only one which could raise doubts about our determination, while all others speak in favor of its correctness.

4, c. γ. The Ro.

The measure Ro has already appeared to us as the smallest part of the bše divided into 320 parts in the mathematical Papyrus Rhind, and we have noted that, although it is never named there, it also occurs in our papyrus. We will now have to substantiate this. Its — that is, the Ro's — use in the hermetic book that compiles the remedies of Egyptian medicine — for that is what the Pap. Ebers is — was to be expected from the outset. The knowledge of prescriptions of the Egyptians, for whose refined development our manuscript provides such brilliant testimony, did not remain the exclusive property of the physicians active on the Nile; rather, it was observed from them by learned Greek physicians in Alexandria and transferred into the pharmacological science of the Hellenes. And even though it has not yet been very long since

von denen ihre Schriften voll sind, so werden sie sich jetzt gezwungen
sehen diese mit Gelehrsamkeit und Klopffechterkunst, doch geringem
Scharfblick vertheidigte Meinung zurückzunehmen. Die bekannte Zart-
lichkeit für die Originalität des griechischen Geistes, der nach ihrer
Ansicht Schaden genommen hätte, wenn er nicht auf sämtlichen Ge-
bieten seiner Bethätigung von allem Fremden freigeblieben wäre, hatte
sie dahin geführt, die Hellenen, deren offener Blick uns doch hell und
aufmerkend genug aus ihren Werken entgegenschaut, für blöde und
kurzsichtig zu halten; denn das wären sie gewesen, wenn sie in der
That die Augen vor den in ihrer unmittelbaren Nähe aufgespeicherten
Wissensschätzen der Aegypter verschlossen hätten, sei es in Folge des
Unvermögens eine fremde Sprache zu erlernen, sei es aus Furcht oder
Abneigung was auch immer von einem barbarischen Volk zu entlehnen.
Aber hören wir nicht häufig genug von den Dolmetschern oder Herme-
neuten sprechen, welche seit dem Beginn der XXVI. Dynastie, von

dem hellenistischen Aegypten schon von den ersten Ptolemäern an
das Griechische unter den Nationalaegyptern Umgangssprache war und
von aller Welt, also auch sicherlich von den Gelehrten, verstanden
und geredet wurde? Und was es mit jener «Abneigung» auf sich hat,

welche hervorragende Führer des geistigen Lebens in Griechenland
von Thales, dem Haupte der frühen ionischen Schule, von Pythagoras
und Plato an bis in verhältnismässig späte Zeit der aegyptischen

that European and above all English scholars of distinction attempted to demonstrate that the Greek scholars who worked in Alexandria as members of the Museum or independently, following a new method and achieving great things especially in the natural sciences, mathematics, and mechanics, did so entirely uninfluenced by their native Egyptian colleagues, without looking around in their immediate vicinity, and far from borrowing anything whatsoever from the Egyptians, relying entirely on themselves and arriving from within themselves at the astonishing advances of which their writings are full — they will now find themselves compelled to abandon this opinion, which they defended with erudition and polemical skill but little discernment. The well-known tenderness for the originality of the Greek mind, which in their view would have suffered had it not remained free from all foreign influence in every area of its activity, had led them to regard the Hellenes — whose open gaze looks out at us brightly and attentively from their works — as dull and short-sighted; for that is what they would have been, had they in fact closed their eyes to the stores of knowledge of the Egyptians accumulated in their immediate vicinity, whether due to an inability to learn a foreign language, or out of fear or reluctance to borrow anything from a barbarian people. But do we not hear frequently enough of interpreters or hermeneutai, who from the beginning of the XXVI Dynasty, from Psamtik I onward into Roman times, were to be found everywhere along the Nile as intermediaries between Egyptians and Hellenes? Do we not know that in Hellenistic Egypt, from the first Ptolemies onward, Greek was the common spoken language among native Egyptians, and was understood and spoken by everyone, and certainly by scholars as well? And as for what lies behind that supposed "reluctance," this is further shown by the admiration, heightened to the point of exaggeration, that leading figures of intellectual life in Greece — from Thales, the head of the early Ionian school, through Pythagoras and Plato, down to comparatively late times — devoted to Egyptian wisdom. Yet even if none of these tributes had come down to us, the specialized research of recent times in the fields of mathematics and metrology would teach us that,

that the Greeks in Alexandria, as we had to expect from the outset, eagerly and gratefully made use of what they found as an old inheritance among their Egyptian fellow researchers; but we cannot better summarize all of this than with the words of Hultsch⁵⁰): "The astonishing knowledge of recipes of the ancient Egyptians, developed down to all its details, was transferred by the Alexandrian physicians into Greek medical science, and indeed just as carefully and systematically as Egyptian geodesy was transmitted through Heron and his successors, of whose activity the surviving remains of Heronian geometry bear sufficient witness." The same Hultsch also showed how the Egyptian apothecary measure was converted into the Attic system in the ratio of 3:2, and how by this calculation the μικρότερον μύστρον of Cleopatra, which according to the original system cannot belong to the Attic Kotyle, was the direct equivalent of the Egyptian Ro. This same measure still appears comparatively late as a fractional measure of a provincial-Roman Kotyle and thus contained ¹⁄₃₂ of the Hin, 0.141 liters⁵¹).

This measure native to Egypt, which recommended itself so strongly to Greek physicians for adoption, was now, as we venture to assert decisively, also frequently taken into account by the author of the Ebers Papyrus. We arrived at this conviction through a more thorough examination of the entire manuscript and first through the careful evaluation of the hieratic sign }, which Stern explained only as a measure for vinegar, beer, and oil. Stern placed this in the mathematical Rhind Papyrus⁵²) among the signs representing fractions of the Ro, and indeed assigned to it the value of ²⁄₃ Ro (¹⁄₄₈ Hin). The question now is whether the Ebers Papyrus confirms this value, and this is indeed the case.

The author of the papyrus took pains, especially where drugs were to be taken in thirds of the measure, to establish the unit. This is also the case with Recipe VI, 19, where, if ℷ, as we presupposed, means ²⁄₃ Ro, then ²⁄₃ Ro of dert (onion?) together with ¹⁄₃ Ro of sweet beer makes one whole Ro. To clarify what has been said, the following notation serves:

dert (onions?) ⁰₁₁₁ . . . . . + = ¹⁄₃ Ro
Sweet beer . . . . . . . . . . ℷ = ²⁄₃ Ro
                         Sum    1 Ro = 0.144 liters.

This is to be drunk, and this circumstance proves that ℷ means at any rate more than ¹⁄₃; for the dert ⁰₁₁₁ was, as its determinative proves, a solid substance, and if it was to be drunk, a quantity of liquid had to be added to it that exceeded its own volume. ¹⁄₂ is ℷ by no means, and so we may, since it also has the value of ²⁄₃ Ro in the Mathematical Papyrus Rhind, hold it with reasonable certainty to mean ²⁄₃ of this measure of capacity.

That the round whole, into which the parts of our recipe combine when ℷ = ²⁄₃ Ro, rests on no mere coincidence, and that the physician was indeed endeavoring to prescribe in such a way that the drugs ordered in ¹⁄₃ Ro together make up 1 full Ro, can be demonstrated through numerous examples, from which it also emerges at the same time that the sign + equals a third of a measure of capacity, and indeed, if nothing deceives us, in most cases of the Ro. It belongs to the weights in no instance, if only because it is not divisible by 2. That the Ro, on the other hand, was divided according to the duodecimal system is shown by its most frequently occurring fractions in the Math. Pap. Rhind: ²⁄₃, ¹⁄₂, ¹⁄₃, ¹⁄₄⁵³⁾.

Of the recipes in which the addition of the parts prescribed in thirds of the Ro yields a whole, only a few shall be cited here in order to support what has been said above:

6. Wo gewogen oder gemessen werden soll.

Aus dem Gesagten geht hervor, dass, wo ganze Zahlen ohne Beigabe eines bestimmten Maasszeichens vorkommen, diese gewöhnlich das Verhältniss der einzelnen Drogen zu einander anzugeben haben. Ein Recept, bei dem hinter den Namen aller vorgeschlagenen Mittel der Strich 1, d. i. die Eins steht, ist zu gleichen Theilen zu nehmen. Die Quantität, welche gewöhnlich von der einzelnen Droge genommen wurde, war gleich dem Ro von 1,41 Centil. Nur hinter der letzten Substanz in der Drogenreihe eines Receptes, dem Bindemittel, gewann der Strich, wie wir unten zeigen werden, gewöhnlich eine andere Bedeutung. Handelte es sich um ganz kleine Dosen, so bediente man sich der 64 Theile des Drachmengewichtes von 6,064 Gramm. Kamen in einem Recepte neben der Eins ganze, diese überschreitende Zahlen vor, galt es gewöhnlich nur die Proportion anzudeuten, in der die Einzelmittel genommen werden sollten. Gab es in der nämlichen Verordnung, wie LXII, 22 — LXIII, 1, ganze Zahlen und Brüche, die in das Gewichtssystem gehörten, so sollten alle Drogen in der Regel gewogen werden. Next follows LXII, 5: black [kohl] 1, stibium 1, water 1, to be ground fine and applied to the eyes. Here the equal parts are again indicated by 3 × the stroke 1; indeed in the next prescription (line 6 ff.) the physician omits the stroke entirely and prescribes: ebony, stibium, and water. Just as we encountered the threefold number of drugs twice just now, we find it often in other places — for example, to mention only one instance, XXVI, 20 and 21, where ox-lung 1, north- or sea-salt 1, and honey 1 are prescribed. The 3 ingredients to be taken in equal parts are to be combined into one and rubbed in with it. This tripartite division again recalls the Ro, which, as was shown above (p. 171 [39]), was readily divided into 3 thirds, whereas the drachma always broke down only into fractions divisible by 2.

6. Where weighing or measuring is to be done.

From what has been said it follows that where whole numbers appear without the addition of a specific unit-sign, these ordinarily indicate the ratio of the individual drugs to one another. A prescription in which the stroke 1 — that is, the numeral one — stands after the name of every suggested ingredient is to be taken in equal parts. The quantity normally taken of an individual drug was equal to the Ro of 1.41 centiliters. Only after the last substance in the list of drugs in a prescription — the binding agent — did the stroke acquire, as we shall show below, a generally different meaning. When very small doses were involved, one made use of the 64 parts of the drachma-weight of 6.064 grams. When in a prescription whole numbers exceeding one appeared alongside the numeral one, it was ordinarily only the proportion in which the individual ingredients were to be taken that was being indicated. If in the same prescription, as in LXII, 22 — LXIII, 1, there were whole numbers and fractions belonging to the system of weights, then as a rule all drugs were to be weighed. As an example we cite LXII, 12 and 13, where first msdmt °⌐⌐⌐ 2 is proposed, and then for other ingredients 1/64, 1/16, 1/8, 1/16. When only fractions of our drachma appear, as in LIV, 6, where the prescription reads: date-powder 1/32, ßnft °⌐⌐⌐ 1/32, ßam ℧⌐ 1/8, ßnê te °⌐⌐⌐ 1/8, then naturally only

Ein einziges Mal soll 1/4 Bier genommen werden, und zwar zusammen mit 1/4 Öl und 1/4 einer anderen Drogue. Wenn hier keine Verschreibung vorliegt und es nicht an allen drei Stellen statt ╳ = 1/4, + = 1/3 heissen muss, was dann eines der häufigen 3 × 1/3 Ro-Recepte ergäbe, so kann uns dies nicht überraschen, weil ja das Ro nach dem Duodecimalsystem getheilt ward, das ebensowohl in Viertel als in Drittel zerfiel. Stände hier statt 1/4 1/3, so würden die 3 verschriebenen Droguen unbedingt zu wägen gewesen sein. Flüssiges wird fast immer gemessen, häufig auch Pulverisiertes; Pflanzentheile, Mineralien und importierte Spezereien werden gewöhnlich gewogen.

Ergebniss. Über die Theilung des Gewichtes, das wir Drachme hiessen, ist das Nöthige gesagt worden. Es enthielt 6,06¼ Gramm und zerfiel in Brüche, deren Zähler 1 und deren Nenner Potenzen von 2 sind. Weiter als bis 1/64 wurde die Theilung nicht geführt; auch hätte die Beschaffenheit der Wagen in alter Zeit dies wahrscheinlich verboten.

Die Theile unserer Drachme sind also: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32, 1/64 und dazu 3/4. Wo — sehen wir von 1/2 und 1/4 ab — diese vorkommen, soll stets gewogen werden. 1/2 war nicht nur von der Gewichtseinheit, sondern auch, und zwar viel häufiger, von dem Ro und ebenso von dem dnât 7 zu nehmen. XXIV, 3 werden verordnet 3 Droguen, von denen je 1/2 Ro zu nehmen war, mit einer Quantität von 7 1/2 zu kochen; dies 7 1/2 aber halten wir nicht für 1½ dnât, sondern für

to be weighed. Only to be measured — and indeed always with the Ro, unless specifically prescribed to use the dnât 7 or Hin — is everything that is to be taken in thirds or sixths. As an example we give LV, 15: crocodile earth 1/3, due (×1)? of dates 1/3, sweet beer 1/2. This recipe belongs to those which teach how readily one rounded up a remedy measured in thirds of the Ro to a whole Ro, by prescribing 1/3 of it. Sometimes both systems were used alongside each other, e.g. XXIII, 4 and 5, where first 1/8 of our drachm each was to be weighed from the śam ꜥꜣ plant and aśd ○ 11 fruit, and then 1/3 Ro of the śypt 1/11 liquid and 1/2 dnât of sweet beer were to be measured. 1/2 is very rarely prescribed by weight, but frequently by volume measure; beer, however, is never weighed but only measured. Only once is 1/4 of beer to be taken, together with 1/4 oil and 1/4 of another drug. If no scribal error is present here and it does not have to read + = 1/3 instead of ╳ = 1/4 at all three places — which would then yield one of the frequent 3 × 1/3 Ro recipes — this need not surprise us, since the Ro was divided according to the duodecimal system, which broke down equally into quarters and thirds. If 1/3 stood here instead of 1/4, the 3 prescribed drugs would necessarily have had to be weighed. Liquids are almost always measured, as are frequently powdered substances; plant parts, minerals, and imported spices are usually weighed.

Result. Regarding the division of the weight that we call the drachm, what is necessary has been said. It contained 6.06¼ grams and broke down into fractions whose numerator is 1 and whose denominators are powers of 2. The division was not carried further than 1/64; moreover, the nature of scales in ancient times would probably have prohibited this.

The parts of our drachm are therefore: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32, 1/64 and in addition 3/4. Where — setting aside 1/2 and 1/4 — these occur, weighing is always to be performed. 1/2 was to be taken not only from the unit of weight, but also, and indeed much more frequently, from the Ro and likewise from the dnât 7. 9. Die Bindemittel und die Steigerung des Werthes der sie begleitenden Zeichen.

Was von Wasser und Bier genommen werden soll, beschliesst ganz regelmässig die Reihe der verordneten Droguen. Häufig treten auch an das Ende derselben Milch, Honig, Öl, Fett, Hefe (serm °ₗₗₗ°), Wein etc. und diese am Schlusse des Receptes stehenden häufigsten Substanzen sind als Bindemittel für die vorhergehenden Droguen zu betrachten. Als Beispiel diene das Recept XLIV, 11—12:

nḳaut °ₗₗₗ° (Mehl?) . . . . ½ Ro
χutẽ °ₗₗₗ° metall . . . . . ½₃₂ Drachme
Frische Datteln . . . . ⅓ Ro
Wasser . . . . . . . . 7 = 1 dnat von 0,608 Centiliter.
Eine Nacht stehen lassen, durchseihen und einen Tag einnehmen.

If we encounter the signs for ½, ═ and 🦢, we will need to examine which measure is meant, and both signs shall receive special consideration further below.

9. The binding agents and the enhancement of the value of the signs accompanying them.

What is to be taken from water and beer regularly concludes the series of prescribed drugs. Frequently milk, honey, oil, fat, yeast (serm °ₗₗₗ°), wine, etc. also appear at the end of these, and these most common substances standing at the close of a recipe are to be regarded as binding agents for the preceding drugs. As an example, let recipe XLIV, 11—12 serve:

nḳaut °ₗₗₗ° (Flour?) . . . . ½ Ro
χutẽ °ₗₗₗ° metal . . . . . 1/32 Drachm

Water . . . . . . . . 7 = 1 dnat of 0.608 centiliters.

Before we compile the division of the dnât 7 and Ro in tabular form, it must be noted that the fractions = ½, + = ⅛, ═ + = ½ ⅓ = ⅙ can refer to both, Ro as well as dnât. It is true that when the hollow measure dnât is to be taken, this is frequently noted specifically by placing the sign 7 next to the fraction, yet this is often omitted after the name of the last drug in a prescription when it is, as usual, the binding agent. In this case the physician knew of himself that more than one part of the Ro was to be taken, and spared himself the writing of the sign for the in any case more voluminous hollow measure used for the apportionment of the binding agent. Since this could be neither the Ro, nor the Hin, nor a weight — for liquids were in general weighed only very rarely — scarcely anything else remains but to regard the fractions which appear after the binding agents at the end of prescriptions, even when no 7 stands beside them, as parts of the dnât 7 of 0.608 liters. This is confirmed especially by the circumstance that wherever alongside the number the measure is also given with which the binding agent is to be measured, this occurs with the help of no other sign than the 7.

10. The last drug in prescriptions to be taken in equal parts.

In the frequent prescriptions in which all drugs are designated with | (1) and are thus to be taken in equal parts, the binding agent also usually stands in the last place; yet in these the stroke, even when it stands after the binding agent, seems only seldom to denote a larger measure, and when it does, not the dnât 7 but rather a Hin.

Aus dem Gesagten ergibt sich also die folgende Regel:
Wo eine Reihe von Droguen, hinter denen allen mit Einschluss der letzten, d. i. des Bindemittels, der Strich steht, das Recept bildet, sollen die einzelnen Substanzen zu je 1 Ro oder ohne nähere Bestimmung „zu gleichen Theilen" genommen werden. Nur in gewissen Fällen, die der Arzt leicht erkannte, war der Strich hinter dem Bindemittel, das die Verordnung abschloss, für ein grösseres Maass, wahrscheinlich für 1 Hin zu halten.

11. Verschiedene Bedeutung des gleichen Zeichens.

Hieraus ergibt sich, dass einige Zeichen einer doppelten Deutung fähig waren; doch konnte diese getrost der Erfahrung des Apothekers überlassen werden. Was das Bindemittel sein sollte wusste er im Voraus und konnte es überdem aus seiner Stellung am Ende des Receptes erkennen. Ein Blick auf die Reihe der verordneten Droguen und die ihrer Aufzählung folgende Angabe wie sie zu behandeln und anzuwenden seien, lehrte ihn, ob der Bruch hinter dem Bindemittel sich auf das Ro oder dnat, der Strich auf das Ro oder Hin beziehe.

Wenn ½ ohne nähere Angabe des Maasses verordnet wird, kann es für die Hälfte des dnat, des Ro oder unserer Drachme angesehen werden, und das Gleiche gilt auch von ¼, wenn dieser Bruch auch am häufigsten in das Gewichtssystem gehört. ⅓ und ⅔ können nur bestimmen, wie viel vom Ro oder dnat verlangt wird. Auf das letztere beziehen sich die genannten Brüche indessen nur, wenn das 𓏲 sie begleitet oder wenn sie hinter dem Namen eines Bindemittels am Ende des Receptes stehen. Die Einheit, der Strich |, deutet gewöhnlich auf das Ro, hinter dem Bindemittel am Schluss der Verordnung aber auch bisweilen auf das Hin.

Somit wären denn alle vorkommenden Maasszeichen bestimmt, und es liegt uns nur noch ob zu untersuchen, wie sich 𓌀 und ⟹ unterscheiden, von denen wir wissen, dass sie beide ½ bedeuten.

59] Pap. Ebers. The Measures and the Chapter on Eye Diseases. 191

could come to be ground up. If, on the other hand, one assumes that the stroke | after the binding agent beef tallow signifies a Hin of 0.456 liters, this would correspond well to the 32 Ro = 0.451 liters of the hard substances listed alongside the Hin of beef tallow, the Ro of oil and goose fat, from which the ointment is to be compounded.

From what has been said, the following rule emerges:
Where a series of drugs — behind all of which, including the last, i.e. the binding agent, the stroke stands — forms the prescription, the individual substances are to be taken at 1 Ro each, or without further specification "in equal parts." Only in certain cases, which the physician would easily recognize, was the stroke after the binding agent that concluded the prescription to be understood as a larger measure, probably 1 Hin.

11. The Various Meanings of the Same Sign.

From this it follows that some signs were capable of a double interpretation; yet this could safely be left to the experience of the apothecary. He knew in advance what the binding agent was to be, and could furthermore recognize it from its position at the end of the prescription. A glance at the series of prescribed drugs and the instruction following their enumeration as to how they were to be prepared and applied taught him whether the fraction after the binding agent referred to the Ro or the dnat, and the stroke to the Ro or the Hin.

When ½ is prescribed without further specification of the measure, it can be understood as half of the dnat, the Ro, or our drachm; and the same applies to ¼, even though this fraction most frequently belongs to the weight system. ⅓ and ⅔ can only determine how much of the Ro or dnat is required. The fractions mentioned relate to the latter, however, only when the sign 𓏲 accompanies them, or when they appear after the name of a binding agent at the end of the prescription. The unit, the stroke |, usually refers to the Ro, but after the binding agent at the conclusion of the prescription it sometimes also refers to the Hin.

Thus all the occurring measure signs would be accounted for, and it remains only for us to investigate how 𓌀 and ⟹ differ from one another, of which we know that both mean ½.

12. Würdigung der ½ bedeutenden Zeichen ⌐ und 𓅱.

Von vorn herein ergibt sich, dass das Wasser als Bindemittel 13mal dem Zeichen 𓅱 = ½, nie dem ⌐ vorangeht. Die einzige Ausnahme bildet das oben erwähnte Beispiel LXXXIX, 16, wo das ⌐ sicher als besonderes Wassermaass zu betrachten ist, das wahrscheinlich sogar das dnat an Grösse überbot. In den anderen Recepten tritt das Bindemittel, von dem die Hälfte zu nehmen ist, in Begleitung nicht des ⌐, sondern 𓅱 an den Schluss zuerst von Droguereihen, die mit dem Ro zu messen sind, wie XVI, 19—20, wo von oberaegyptischem Durrakorn ⅓ Ro, von Seesalz ⅔ Ro und von Wasser 𓅱 genommen werden soll. Als Bindemittel für nur zu Wägendes tritt das Wasser 𓅱 = ½ z. B. in den Recepten XLV, 8 und 9 auf, wo ihm Drogen, die mit ⅛, ¼, ¹⁄₁₆, ¹⁄₂₂, ¼, ¹⁄₃₂ zu wiegen sind, vorangehen. Das Gleiche gilt von den Recepten XLV, 9—10, 16—18, 18—20, 20—22; L, 10—11. Theils zu Wägendes, theils zu Messendes soll z. B. LI, 8 und 9 durch 𓅱 = ½ Wasser gebunden werden. Die vorgeschriebenen Maasse lauten dort ½ ½ = ⅝ Ro, ¼, 2 × ¹⁄₃₂ Drachme und Wasser 𓅱 = ½. Hier könnte 𓅱 in einigen Fällen zwar zwanglos für ½ Ro gehalten werden, z. B. XVI, 20, wo ½ Ro Wasser ein genügendes Bindemittel für ⅓ Ro Korn und ⅔ Ro Seesalz sein würde⁶⁹), doch auch hier findet der Pharmaceut die vorgeschlagene Dosis spärlich. Fast überall sieht man sich genöthigt an eine grössere Quantität zu denken; und diese Forderung wird neu bestätigt durch das Bier, das gleichfalls recht oft als Bindemittel, und zwar mit dem 𓅱 = ½ genommen werden soll. Dass dies 𓅱 neben dem Bier mehr als ½ Ro bedeutet, scheint sicher belegt zu werden z. B. durch III, 4, wo verordnet wird die vorangehenden Drogen mit 𓅱 = ½ Bier

69) Bei XLIV, 7, wo thbu ⟹ Holz 𓅱 = ½, ½ Ro Milch, ¹⁄₃₂ Drachme Honig und Wasser 𓅱 = ½ verordnet wird, kann das 𓅱 in der Mitte und am Ende des Receptes sehr wohl dasselbe, ja, wegen des + = ½ Milch auch ½ Ro bedeuten. Weil das Ganze aber zu kochen ist, empfiehlt es sich wohl auch hier das zweite 𓅱 für die Hälfte eines grösseren Maasses anzusehen.

12. Assessment of the ½-significant signs ⌐ and 𓅱.

It is immediately apparent that water, as a binding agent, precedes the sign 𓅱 = ½ thirteen times, and never precedes ⌐. The sole exception is the example mentioned above at LXXXIX, 16, where ⌐ is certainly to be regarded as a special water measure, which probably even exceeded the dnat in size. In the other prescriptions, the binding agent of which half is to be taken appears not with ⌐ but with 𓅱 at the end of lists of drugs to be measured by the Ro, as in XVI, 19–20, where one is to take ⅓ Ro of Upper Egyptian durra grain, ⅔ Ro of sea salt, and water 𓅱. As a binding agent for ingredients to be weighed only, water 𓅱 = ½ appears, for example, in prescriptions XLV, 8 and 9, where it is preceded by drugs to be weighed in amounts of ⅛, ¼, ¹⁄₁₆, ¹⁄₂₂, ¼, ¹⁄₃₂. The same applies to prescriptions XLV, 9–10, 16–18, 18–20, 20–22; L, 10–11. Ingredients partly to be weighed and partly to be measured are, for example in LI, 8 and 9, to be bound with 𓅱 = ½ water. The prescribed quantities there read ½ ½ = ⅝ Ro, ¼, 2 × ¹⁄₃₂ drachma, and water 𓅱 = ½. Here 𓅱 could in some cases without difficulty be taken to mean ½ Ro, e.g. in XVI, 20, where ½ Ro of water would be a sufficient binding agent for ⅓ Ro of grain and ⅔ Ro of sea salt⁶⁹), yet even here the pharmacist finds the proposed dose meager. Almost everywhere one feels compelled to think of a larger quantity; and this requirement is newly confirmed by beer, which likewise is quite often to be taken as a binding agent, namely with 𓅱 = ½. That this 𓅱 alongside beer signifies more than ½ Ro seems to be securely attested, for example by III, 4, where it is prescribed that the preceding drugs be bound with 𓅱 = ½ beer.

69) In XLIV, 7, where thbu ⟹ wood 𓅱 = ½, ½ Ro milk, ¹⁄₃₂ drachma honey, and water 𓅱 = ½ are prescribed, the 𓅱 in the middle and at the end of the prescription can very well mean the same thing, and indeed, on account of + = ½ milk, also ½ Ro. But since the whole is to be cooked, it is advisable here too to regard the second 𓅱 as denoting half of a larger measure.

oder ⅓ Wein zu trinken. Hier kann weder bei der ersten noch zweiten Flüssigkeit an ⅓ Ro gedacht werden; der Arzt meint viel-mehr sehr wahrscheinlich das dnât 7, das er nur zu bezeichnen unterlässt. Auch XL, 18 sollen drei, je zu ¼ Drachme zu nehmende Droguen stehen gelassen und mit süssem Bier 𓎆 = ½ getrunken werden. Hier muss ebenfalls die Hälfte eines grösseren Maasses als des Ro gemeint sein, wie der Pharmaceut auf den ersten Blick erkennt. Das Hin kommt kaum in Frage, weil es nicht in Drittel zerfällt, während das dnât 7 wie das Ro mit gleichem Recht in Halbe wie in Drittel getheilt werden kann. Für das dnât 7 spricht auch die sonstige Messung des Wassers wie des Bieres als Bindemittel am Schluss der Recepte; denn XLIV finden sich drei solche, in denen allen am Schluss der Drogüenreihe ein ganzes dnât Wasser als Binde-mittel verordnet wird. Das Gleiche gilt von XLIX, 4 und LXVII, 16. Auch ½ dnât 7 Wasser und Bier werden oft in Begleitung des 7 am Schluss des Receptes vorgeschrieben; so sollen XIV, 12—16 4 Sub-stanzen mit 1/15, ⅛, ¼ und 5/16 Drachme gewogen werden. Als Binde-mittel folgt dann Wasser 7+ = ⅓ dnât. Auf derselben Seite Z. 21 beschliesst wiederum Wasser 7+ = ½ dnât die Verordnung. Beim Biere wird, wenn vom Bindemittel ein ganzes oder ⅓ dnât zu nehmen ist, noch seltener unterlassen das Zeichen 7 zu benutzen und es ent-weder mit der Bedeutung 1 ganzes dnât allein oder mit dem Werthe ½ dnât 7+ zu schreiben.

XVII, 14—18 sollen z. B. 2 Pflanzenstoffe zu ⅓ genommen und ihnen dann ein dnât 7 süssen Bieres beigemischt werden. Die Drittel sind als Ro zu fassen, während von dem Bindemittel Bier sehr viel mehr, 1 dnât verordnet wird. XXII, 18—19 sollen 7 consistente Sub-stanzen gewogen und nur von der Pflanze snut 𓇛 5/16 und dem àmemu 𓇛₁₁ samen ⅓ Ro genommen werden. Mit 1 dnât 7 süssen Bieres schliesst endlich das Ganze, das zu kochen ist. XLIII, 9 ff. sollen 15 Stoffe gewogen werden, mitten unter ihnen wird (12) von Wein ⅓ Ro zu nehmen verordnet, und das ganze siebzehntheilige Recept schliesst mit dem Bindemittel Bier, wovon 7+ = ⅓ dnât vorgeschrieben wird. Bei dem viertheiligen Recept XII, 5—8 tritt ausnahmsweise das Binde-
