or ⅓ wine to drink. Here neither for the first nor the second liquid can ⅓ Ro be intended; the physician most likely means the dnât 7, which he merely omits to indicate. Also in XL, 18, three drugs, each to be taken in ¼ drachm, are to be left standing and drunk with sweet beer 𓎆 = ½. Here too the half of a measure larger than the Ro must be intended, as any pharmacist recognizes at first glance. The Hin is hardly in question, since it does not divide into thirds, whereas the dnât 7, like the Ro, can equally well be divided into halves as into thirds. In favor of the dnât 7 speaks also the usual measurement of water and beer as binding agents at the end of the prescriptions; for in XLIV there are three such cases, in all of which at the end of the series of drugs one whole dnât of water is prescribed as the binding agent. The same applies to XLIX, 4 and LXVII, 16. Also ½ dnât 7 of water and beer are often prescribed together with the 7 at the end of prescriptions; thus in XIV, 12–16, 4 substances are to be weighed in amounts of 1/15, ⅛, ¼, and 5/16 drachm. As a binding agent there follows Water 7+ = ⅓ dnât. On the same page, line 21, Water 7+ = ½ dnât again concludes the prescription. With beer, when the binding agent requires one whole or ⅓ dnât, it is even less frequently omitted to use the sign 7, writing it either with the meaning of 1 whole dnât alone, or with the value ½ dnât as 7+.

In XVII, 14–18, for example, 2 plant substances are to be taken in ⅓ each, and then one dnât 7 of sweet beer is to be mixed with them. The thirds are to be understood as Ro, while for the binding agent beer a much larger quantity, 1 dnât, is prescribed. In XXII, 18–19, 7 solid substances are to be weighed, and only from the plant snut 𓇛 5/16 and from the àmemu 𓇛₁₁ seed ⅓ Ro is to be taken. With 1 dnât 7 of sweet beer the whole thing, which is to be cooked, is finally concluded. In XLIII, 9 ff., 15 substances are to be weighed; among them, at position (12), ⅓ Ro of wine is prescribed, and the entire seventeen-part prescription closes with the binding agent beer, of which 7+ = ⅓ dnât is specified. In the four-part prescription XII, 5–8, the binding agent exceptionally appears—

So sehen wir denn, dass das 𓆤 hinter den die einzelnen Drogen verschmelzenden Flüssigkeiten in das Dnâtsystem gehört und in demselben ½ bedeutet, — während das 〓, das LXXXIX, 46 ganz

means Beer 7+ = ½ dnât not at the end, but at the head of the row of other drugs. Otherwise, the beer to be used as a binding agent at ⅓ dnât 7 appears everywhere at the end of the prescription. So also in XXIII, 3. 7. 9. 21. XXIV, 11. XXXVI, 3. XLIV, 6. XLV, 23. LI, 3. 11. 14. LII, 17. XCIII, 9. Just as the dnât 7 is everywhere the measure by which the binding agent is to be measured, so too the physician will have thought of the dnât 7 when he prescribed only 𓆤 = ½ of the binding agent. Even without writing the 7 he was understood, and that we are to see in this 𓆤 after the last drug of the prescription only ½ dnât 7, and not half of some other measure, is already evident from the fact that we find 7+ quite often, but 7𓆤 only once as a measure of the most common binding agent, water, namely in XXIV, 3, where 3 ingredients are measured with the Ro and are to be boiled with a quantity of 7𓆤 water. With beer the 𓆤 is never more precisely defined by the sign 7, and so we would have to assume that of a measure of which one very often took ⅓, one would never have prescribed a half, if we could not bring ourselves to see in 𓆤 ½ dnât 7. But everything compels us to do this, and we are convinced that where the bare 𓆤 stands after the binding agent beer at the end of the prescription, it is equally to be taken as ½ dnât as if it had received a more precise definition through the 7.

We remain undecided regarding prescription XLIV, 20–21, where after 4 plant substances to be weighed, of fresh porridge or dough, 3=𓆤 = ½ and 4 dnât 7 of water is prescribed. Here too it is more probable that ½ dnât is meant rather than ½ Ro. The 7 after the water presumably refers also to the directly preceding eb 𓇳𓏏𓏏𓏏 ut 𓆤, i.e. fresh porridge or dough ½.

65] Pap. Ebers. Die Maasse u. das Kapitel über die Augenkrankheiten. 497

griechischen und römischen Ärzten gewann, spricht für seine Verwendbarkeit auch unter den Aegyptern. Ausserdem wird kein kleinerer Theil als ¼ des Ro verordnet, und wir sehen keinen Weg, das von uns für 1 Ro erklärte Maass anders zu bestimmen als es geschehen ist. Bei den zahlreichen Recepten, in denen den Namen sämmtlicher Droguen der Strich | folgt, und die also zu gleichen Theilen zu nehmen sind, lässt sich weder das dnât 7 noch das Hin ℌ als Einheit denken, auch die Drachme kommt kaum in Frage, sicher nicht bei solchen Mitteln, die zu ⅓, ⅔ und ¾ genommen werden sollen. Für die zu gleichen Theilen herzustellenden Recepte wären wie dnât 7 so Hin ℌ viel zu gross, und neben ihnen muss unbedingt ein sehr viel kleineres Hohlmaass verwandt worden sein, das nach dem Duodecimalsystem und mit Vorliebe in Drittel zertheilt ward. Dies konnte sich nie und nimmer auf das Drachmengewicht beziehen, weil dies eben nur in Brüche zerfällt, deren Zähler 1 ist und deren Nenner Potenzen von 2 sind. So wird wohl das Ro, dessen Name ebensowenig genannt wird wie der des Drachmengewichtes, denjenigen Werth erhalten dürfen, den wir ihm nach Berücksichtigung seines Vorkommens an allen Stellen des Papyrus zuertheilt haben.

Bei der nun folgenden Umschrift und Übersetzung des den Augenkrankheiten gewidmeten Kapitels werden wir uns der folgenden Abkürzungen bedienen:

Die Drachme = D.
Das Hin = H.
Das Ḥnu = H̱.
Das Dnât = 7.
Das Ro = R.

Wo wir keine sichere Deutung für die Namen der vorgeschlagenen Medicamente gefunden, wird sie ein? begleiten. Eine ihnen gewidmete, nächstens von uns zu veröffentlichende monographische Arbeit wird hoffentlich manches zu relativer Gewissheit erheben, was wir jetzt noch nicht zu bestimmen wagten.

Berichtigung. S. 448 Z. 6 von oben lies: H.L. statt ḥnu.

translation:
65] Pap. Ebers. The Measures and the Chapter on Eye Diseases. 497

that it gained among Greek and Roman physicians speaks for its usefulness also among the Egyptians. Moreover, no smaller portion than ¼ of the Ro is prescribed, and we see no way to determine the measure we have identified as 1 Ro other than as it has been done. In the numerous recipes in which the names of all drugs are followed by the stroke |, and which are therefore to be taken in equal parts, neither the dnât 7 nor the Hin ℌ can be conceived of as a unit; the drachm also hardly comes into question, certainly not for those remedies that are to be taken in ⅓, ⅔, and ¾ portions. For recipes to be prepared in equal parts, both the dnât 7 and the Hin ℌ would be far too large, and alongside them a much smaller hollow measure must certainly have been used, one that was divided according to the duodecimal system and preferably into thirds. This could never under any circumstances refer to the drachm weight, because the latter breaks down only into fractions whose numerators are 1 and whose denominators are powers of 2. Thus the Ro, whose name is mentioned just as rarely as that of the drachm weight, will rightly receive the value that we assigned to it after considering all its occurrences throughout the papyrus.

In the transcription and translation of the chapter devoted to eye diseases that follows, we will use the following abbreviations:

The Drachm = D.
The Hin = H.
The Ḥnu = H̱.
The Dnât = 7.
The Ro = R.

Where we have found no certain interpretation for the names of the proposed medicaments, it will be accompanied by a question mark. A monographic work devoted to these matters, which we will shortly publish, will hopefully raise a number of points to relative certainty that we did not yet venture to determine at present.

Hirschberg, Wörterbuch der Augenheilkunde, übersetzt das Staphylom (σταφύλωμα) zutreffend »Beerengeschwulst«. Celsus VII, 7, 11 sagt: »Im Auge selbst wächst bisweilen die oberste Haut empor (attollitur), indem entweder in Innern einige Häute reissen oder sich ausdehnen. Dadurch entsteht ein Bild, das dem einer Weinbeere gleicht, woher die Griechen dies auch σταφύλωμα heissen«. Nach Hirschberg bedeutet es uns nur Hervorwölbung oder Wulst, und die aegyptischen Ärzte, die dergleichen entstehen sahen, konnten es leicht das krankhafte Wachsen nennen. 9) Dr. Schneider in Leipzig, as well as Dr. Schmidt in Wiesbaden, who always showed himself ready to support me most effectively with valuable advice, both thought it possible to recognize in the pathological growth or growth-disease of the eye what we call staphyloma, in which the cornea bulges outward and thus appears to grow. Hirschberg, Dictionary of Ophthalmology, aptly translates staphyloma (σταφύλωμα) as "berry-swelling." Celsus VII, 7, 11 says: "In the eye itself the outermost membrane sometimes grows upward (attollitur), while inwardly certain membranes tear or expand. This produces an image resembling a grape, which is why the Greeks call it σταφύλωμα." According to Hirschberg it signifies for us only a protrusion or bulge, and the Egyptian physicians, who saw such things develop, could easily have called it a pathological growth. The word attollitur in Celsus shows that the growing upward seemed characteristic to him as well.

10) In the red color with which the Egyptian scribes marked the beginnings of sentences, while they used black ink for the running text, the chemical analysis of Dr. Christen found red lead. This was also preserved in the indentations on several scribal palettes. It is a lead oxide, occurring on cerussite and galena crystals.

11) ⌐ ° uetu ° With this substance one is to paint green, to write, and to paint the eye. It is also written ⌐ uet or ⌐ uet ☐. In Leps. Denku. there occurs at II, 92e the variant ⌐ uet ° °°° which designates uet as intended for the eye. Further below in our Papyrus LX, 17 and 18 we will come to know uetu ° as one of those excellent drugs which were described as outflows from the eye of Horus. It must have been green; for it says there: come, come uetu °, come green one, etc. Its name also denotes green and the green color, like the Coptic oyωτ, corresponding to the old uet, meaning green, oyoτoyeτ as infinitive and as a noun the Green. interesting compound [hieroglyphic signs] uetu ° hmy ° green parts of copper
appear. It is now necessary to search among the minerals for green copper compounds (copper salts) which could correspond to our ueta. There are quite a few of these, as our dear colleague, the excellent mineralogist Professor F. Zinkel, informs us, even apart from verdigris, which does not occur as a mineral. Phosphorchalcite, Libethenite, Tagilite, the water-containing arsenic-acid copper minerals Olivenite, Euchroite, Strahlerz, the water-containing sulfuric-acid copper mineral Brochantite, and the water-poor vanadium-acid limestone copper Volborthite were probably not in the hands of the ancients, all of which are green. Present in antiquity were Malachite, i.e. basic carbonate of copper, and water-containing siliceous copper. This too was green, and it seems as though scarcely anything else could be meant by ueta. One can hardly think of Malachite or verdigris; for although the latter is frequently mentioned, and a few small antiques made of this mineral have survived (e.g. a pile-dwelling statuette in Dresden), its name msfkt ° never alternates with our ueta °, although this certainly means "that which is green." Verdigris was found in tombs, but it certainly did not need to be imported from abroad. Used adjectivally, uet serves to designate the green color of the sea, of crops, and of artworks on which the green color has been preserved. On the Sinai Peninsula were the mines from which the Egyptians obtained Malachite, which was also frequently brought to them as tribute by Asiatic peoples, and the ueta-mineral; for this (determined with [sign], and thereby designated as stone), is named as a product of the land of Bẓ, i.e. of Petraic Arabia and later also of Persia. The water-containing siliceous copper could have had the same homeland, was green and fulfilled the conditions we must require of the uetu. We therefore consider ourselves justified in naming it Siliceous Copper, i.e. water-containing silicic-acid copper, though with a † as a mark of critical caution.

The second person, which often appears in emphatic speech,

LVIII, 7 and 8, the word χnnu is also used
for the storm that breaks out in the sky or comes in
from the sky of the north. It is hardly possible, as Brugsch suggests, to connect it
with the Coptic ϣⲱⲛⲧ, ϣⲱⲛⲉ meaning infirmum esse, labor, πόνος.
We would rather compare it with ϣⲱⲛⲧ adpropinquare, ingruere,
which fits LVIII, 7—8 exactly, were it not for the radical t in
ϣⲱⲛⲧ. That it expresses something violent is already shown
by the determinatives, and our word is sometimes also used to denote
unrest, revolt, and the like in political life. Examples
are found in Brugsch's Dictionary, Ser. II, p. 934—35. On Plate 2
of J. Dümichen's treatment of the building records of the Temple of Edfu,

relate to the cornea of the patient, which, when his eye is
seized by staphyloma, sometimes tears. This had already been
recognized by the ancients. Aëtius (540 A.D.), p. 130, distinguishes staphyloma without
and with tearing of the cornea. Nevertheless, the interpretation
presented here is insufficiently supported, which is why it is best to remain
with the one given above.

text:
75] Pap. Ebers. Die Maasse u. das Kapitel über die Augenkrankheiten. 207

Schon in der XII. Dyn. sehen wir msdmt (dort msṯmt [hieratic signs] geschrieben) von Semiten nach Aegypten einführen. In der XVIII. Dyn. wird es unter den Droguen erwähnt, welche die Flotte der Hatspsu aus Punt (die Arabia Felix oder Somaliküste) nach Aegypten brachte. Dümichen, Flotte einer aeg. Königin, p. 2. Es ward zur Salbe καὶ ἐξοχήν, und in der sprachlichen Form [hieratic signs] stm [hieratic signs] diente es in der Zeit der Niederschrift unseres Pap. (XVIII. Dyn.) zur Bezeichnung von Salbe und salben überhaupt. Später brauchte man dann das gleiche Wort, da sich in den meisten Salben Stibium befand, zur Bezeichnung dieses Minerales, das auf koptisch S. стнм, B. соnм heisst und dem stimmi oder stibi entspricht, das nach Plinius hist. nat. 33, 101 nebst alabastrum und larbasis der aeg. Name für Antimon war. Das griechische στίμμις ward auch von Eustathius zur Odyssee als aeg. Wort bezeichnet καὶ τὴν μέλαιναν στίμμιν ὀμματογράφον, auch das schwarze augenfärbende Stimmis. Nach Plinius ist es eine Art von Spiessglas, das gebrannt oder gedörrt pulverisirt wird, um die Augenränder damit zu schwärzen. Über diese Färbung s. Virchow's »Altaegyptische Augenschwärze«. Verhandlungen der Berl. Gesellsch. für Anthropologie, Ethnologie etc. 26. Mai 1888 und später meine Bemerkungen l. l. 1889, S. 574 ff. Bei Dioscorides v. 99 ed. Kühn, werden alle Eigenschaften dieses Metalles aufgezählt, das στίμμι genannt wird. Man nannte es auch πλατυόφθαιμον, λάρβασον, γυναικεῖον, das weibliche und χαλκηδόνιον⁷⁷ᵃ). Unter anderem diente es dazu, Unreinheiten und Schwären oder Schäden (ἕλκος = ulcus) zu beseitigen und um die Augen zu reinigen. »Im Ganzen ist seine Wirkung ähnlich dem gebrannten Blei.« Diese Notiz ist wichtig; denn in der That scheint man in Aegypten, wo das Stibium oder Antimon schwer zu erlangen war, sich eine gute Augenschwärze verschafft zu haben, indem man Kohle mit schwefelsaurem Blei glühte. Es sind nämlich zu Azmim in Oberaegypten bei einigen Mumien kleine Säckchen mit Augenschwärze gefunden worden; diese, ein feines Pulver, hatte der berühmte Nachfolger Liebig's, Prof. von Baeyer in München, die Güte für uns zu analysieren. Seine Mit-

17a) Wie Dioscor. die weibliche, so erwähnt und beschreibt Plinius die »Männchen« (mas) und »Weibchen« (femina) genannten Stibiumsorten.
translation:
75] Pap. Ebers. The Measures and the Chapter on Eye Diseases. 207

Already in the 12th Dynasty we see msdmt (there written msṯmt [hieratic signs]) being imported by Semites into Egypt. In the 18th Dynasty it is mentioned among the drugs which the fleet of Hatshepsut brought to Egypt from Punt (Arabia Felix or the Somali coast). Dümichen, Fleet of an Egyptian Queen, p. 2. It was used as a salve par excellence, and in the linguistic form [hieratic signs] stm [hieratic signs] it served during the time of the writing of our Papyrus (18th Dynasty) to designate ointment and anointing in general. Later the same word was used, since most ointments contained stibium, to designate this mineral, which in Coptic S. is стнм, B. соnм, and which corresponds to stimmi or stibi, which according to Pliny hist. nat. 33, 101, along with alabastrum and larbasis, was the Egyptian name for antimony. The Greek στίμμις was also identified by Eustathius in his commentary on the Odyssey as an Egyptian word: καὶ τὴν μέλαιναν στίμμιν ὀμματογράφον, also the black eye-coloring Stimmis. According to Pliny it is a type of stibnite, which is burned or dried and powdered, to blacken the edges of the eyes with it. On this coloring see Virchow's "Old Egyptian Eye-black." Proceedings of the Berlin Society for Anthropology, Ethnology etc., 26 May 1888 and later my remarks ibid. 1889, p. 574 ff. In Dioscorides v. 99 ed. Kühn, all the properties of this metal are enumerated, where it is called στίμμι. It was also called πλατυόφθαιμον, λάρβασον, γυναικεῖον, the feminine, and χαλκηδόνιον⁷⁷ᵃ). Among other things it served to remove impurities and sores or lesions (ἕλκος = ulcus) and to cleanse the eyes. "In general its effect is similar to burnt lead." This note is important; for it appears that in Egypt, where stibium or antimony was hard to obtain, people procured a good eye-black by heating coal with lead sulfate. Indeed, in Azmim in Upper Egypt, small pouches of eye-black have been found with some mummies; these, a fine powder, were kindly analyzed for us by the famous successor of Liebig, Prof. von Baeyer in Munich. His com-

208 Georg Ebers, [76

theilung lehrt, dass es aus Kohle und Schwefelblei besteht. Daneben befinden sich einige Spuren von Holz und Magnesia, sowie Sand; doch können die letzteren Substanzen als zufällige Verunreinigungen angesehen werden. »Aller Wahrscheinlichkeit nach«, schreibt Prof. v. Baeyer, »ist das Pulver durch Glühen von Kohle mit schwefelsaurem Blei erhalten worden. Ich habe diese beiden Ingredienzien durch Glühen in ein ganz ähnliches Pulver verwandelt, welches genau dieselben Eigenschaften zeigte. Es fragt sich nun: Wie kamen die Aegypter zu schwefelsaurem Blei? Diese Substanz findet sich in der Natur als Bleivitriol; ich weiss aber nicht, ob dies Mineral in Aegypten vorkommt. Übrigens konnte man es auch künstlich bereitet haben. Blei, das sie schon kannten, gibt beim Erhitzen an der Luft Bleiglätte (Lithargyrum), dies löst sich in Essig auf, und auf Zusatz von Alaun erhält man dann schwefelsaures Blei als Niederschlag. Die Beimengung von Sand und Eisen machen es aber wahrscheinlicher, dass das Mineral Bleivitriol zur Bereitung gedient hat. Von Stibium fand sich keine Spur.« Magnesia, dies sei hierzu bemerkt, gab es schon in Aegypten. Im Leydener gnostischen Papyrus, verso II, 7 ff. wird sie erwähnt und bemerkt, dass sie dem stm (Stibium) ähnlich sei, welches, wenn man es zerstosse, schwarz werde. Die Analyse der Schwärzen von Azmim und anderer erhaltener Augenschwärzen z. B. einiger Proben aus Berlin und Turin ergab gar kein Stibium, und so lässt sich annehmen, dass man sich gewöhnlich eines falschen Stibiums bediente, welches man erhielt, indem man Kohle mit schwefelsaurem Blei glühte. Das wird das falsche Msdmt gewesen sein, welches neben dem ächten »méat« gebraucht worden sein muss, das LVIII, 18 und LIX, 6 verordnet wird. Es findet sich auch in der indischen medicinischen Litteratur oft erwähnt.

18) Verschleierung, eigentlich Verhüllung, Bedeckung, auch determinirt mit dem einem Mann im Verstecke, der stets auf Verborgenes und Verdecktes weist. Eine iritistische Affection ist hier sehr wahrscheinlich gemeint, weil in Verbindung mit ihr von einem Blutaustritt die Rede ist, so LVII, 6—8.

208 Georg Ebers, [76

analysis teaches that it consists of carbon and lead sulfide. Besides, there are some traces of wood and magnesia, as well as sand; however, the latter substances can be regarded as accidental impurities. "In all probability," writes Prof. v. Baeyer, "the powder was obtained by heating carbon with lead sulfate. I have transformed these two ingredients by heating into a very similar powder, which showed exactly the same properties. The question now arises: How did the Egyptians obtain lead sulfate? This substance occurs in nature as lead vitriol; I do not know, however, whether this mineral occurs in Egypt. Moreover, it could also have been artificially prepared. Lead, which they already knew, when heated in air gives lead oxide (litharge), which dissolves in vinegar, and upon the addition of alum one then obtains lead sulfate as a precipitate. The admixture of sand and iron makes it more likely, however, that the mineral lead vitriol served for the preparation. No trace of stibium was found." Magnesia, it should be noted here, was already present in Egypt. In the Leiden Gnostic Papyrus, verso II, 7 ff., it is mentioned and noted that it resembles the stm (stibium), which turns black when crushed. The analysis of the black pigments from Akhmim and other preserved eye pigments, e.g., from some samples from Berlin and Turin, yielded no stibium at all, and so it may be assumed that one commonly used a false stibium, which was obtained by heating carbon with lead sulfate. That will have been the false Msdmt, which must have been used alongside the genuine "méat," prescribed in LVIII, 18 and LIX, 6. It is also frequently mentioned in Indian medical literature.

Other remedies against the clouding in the eye on the first day. Iritic affection, infiltration of the cornea, beginning cataract formation or the like.

18) Clouding, properly veiling, covering, also determined with the sign of a man in hiding, who always points to things hidden and concealed. An iritic affection is very probably meant here, because in connection with it there is mention of a hemorrhage, as in LVII, 6—8.

212 Georg Ebers, [80

[hieroglyphic symbols] tert [hieroglyphic] or tert [hieroglyphic] — the Onion?

Stern identifies malum citrium (citron) with it, while Batsch tentatively connects it with the Upper Egyptian Coptic zol? cepa (onion). (See ⲏⲕⲱⲗ, B. ⲏⲕⲱⲗ.) This tert [hieroglyphic] is an extraordinarily frequently used remedy, which is weighed, sometimes in larger quantities (¼, ⅛ drachma), and sometimes only in small amounts such as ¹⁄₆₄ drachma. But it is also to be measured, and indeed in fairly large quantities. LIII, 3 prescribes that a rmnt ḥ jug be taken, half filled with water and half with tert [hieroglyphic]. One should allow its contents four days to dry out and settle during the night. When it has clarified to ¼ to ⅛ in the rmnt ḥ jug, it should be given to drink to one who suffers from nausea. It can also be understood as meaning that it should clarify to ⁵⁄₁₂ (¼ ⅛) in the rmnt jug. Should one now take tert [hieroglyphic] to mean onion or citron (malum citreum)? Since zol only in Zoega

thought. The resin of the terebinth (ἄrlw) is especially mentioned by Dioscorides I, 91 p. 94, just as that of the Nile acacia is, and it is said to have been imported from Arabia Petraea and obtained in Judaea, Syria, Cyprus, Libya, and on the Cyclades. Indeed the terebinth resin is declared to be the very best of all: προέχει δὲ πασῶν ῥητίνων ἡ τεριμινθίνη. Dioscorides I, 189 pp. 159 and 60 also counts among medicinal remedies the sap given off by the sycamore trunk. To obtain it, one would score the bark with a cut, and the dried and pastille-formed sap is used in various ways, but chiefly as an emollient. Thus we see the ḏdn of the nḥt [hieroglyphic] or sycamore tree used alongside the ḏdn of the Sunt- and Nebs-trees with other medicines against [hieroglyphic] šnʿ or constipation. Of the Sunt resin ¹⁄₃₂ drachma and of the sycamore sap the same amount are to be taken, and these small doses point to as fine a substance as the dried sap of a tree. We may therefore safely regard the ḏdn, which occurs only in connection with trees, as the dried sap obtained from their trunks. The root meaning of the word, as Batsch demonstrated, is to take the place of something else, to substitute, to transplant; and if we consider that the resin or sap of a tree (certainly that of the sycamore and acacia) was obtained by making incisions in the trunk, which were then filled by the flowing ḏdn, one understands why the Egyptians could call the resin "the filling, the replacing substance."

und wahrscheinlich irrthümlich vorkommt, lassen wir es auf sich beruhen; dagegen spricht für tert die Zwiebel der Umstand, dass die Zwiebel, wie die zahlreichen Bilder auf den Denkmälern und Nachrichten verschiedener Art — man denke nur an IV. Mos. 11, 12, wo die Juden in der Wüste nach בְּצָלִים d. s. Zwiebeln verlangen — eine am Nil sehr viel gebrauchte Frucht war und ist und der zweite, dass wir im ganzen Papyrus kein anderes häufig verordnetes Mittel fanden, das wir für die Zwiebel halten möchten. In der ututut-Pflanze, die Stern für Erbsen hält, möchten wir den in Aegypten sehr häufigen Knoblauch sehen. Plutarchs Behauptung, die aegyptischen Priester hätten die Zwiebel verschmäht, weil sie zum Durste reize, muss auf einem Missverständniss beruhen, denn dazu sieht man sie zu oft als geopfertes Gemüse auf den Altären liegen. In Hern's lehrreichem Werke «Kulturpflanzen und Hausthiere» S. 327 ff. wird die Einführung der Citrone in Europa zu spät gesetzt; denn Herr in Zürich fand Citronenkerne schon in frühen etruskischen Gräbern. In Aegypten war sie wohl zeitig bekannt; und unter den von Thutmes III, 18. Dyn., zu Karnak dargestellten Pflanzen und Früchten (Mariette XXX) ist die eine wohl unsere Citrone. Theophrast's aus der Zeit Alexanders stammende Beschreibung des medischen oder persischen Apfels IV, 4, 2 ist bekannt. Vergil, Georgica III, 126, nennt ihn »felix«. — Jedenfalls gehört die Citrone schon zu den von Dioscorides (1 Jahrh. n. Chr.) vorgeschlagenen Heilmitteln. Er nennt sie μηδικόν scil. μῆλον, κεδρόμηλον und auf lateinisch κίτρια (citria) und setzt ihre allgemeine Bekanntschaft voraus. Seine Beschreibung lässt keinen Zweifel zu, dass die Citrone gemeint sei. Freilich schreibt er ihr weit geringere Heilkraft zu als der Zwiebel. Mit Wein genommen soll sie den Giften entgegen wirken und abführen, gekocht dem Munde angenehmen Athem geben und am häufigsten von den Frauen gegen Appetitlosigkeit und Ekel gebraucht werden (πρὸς τὴν κίσσαν). Endlich soll sie die Kleider vor dem Zerfressenwerden schützen, wenn man sie zu ihnen in die Kiste legt. Das ist Alles; wogegen wir von Dioscorides die Zwiebel in einer Weise anwenden sehen, die für sich genügte, um zu zeigen, dass ihm die aegyptische Therapie, ja vielleicht ein unserem Papyrus ähnliches Werk wohl bekannt war. Sehen wir nun zu, in welchen Verbindungen die tert ° Frucht in unserer Handschrift vorkommt, in welchen Fällen

and which probably appears erroneously, we let it rest; on the other hand, in favor of tert being the onion speaks the circumstance that the onion, as shown by the numerous images on monuments and reports of various kinds — one need only think of Num. 11, 12, where the Jews in the desert demand בְּצָלִים, i.e. onions — was and is a fruit very widely used along the Nile, and second, that throughout the entire papyrus we found no other frequently prescribed remedy that we would wish to consider as the onion. In the ututut-plant, which Stern takes to be peas, we would like to see garlic, which is very common in Egypt. Plutarch's claim that the Egyptian priests disdained the onion because it stimulates thirst must rest on a misunderstanding, for one sees it far too often lying as an offered vegetable on altars. In Hern's instructive work "Cultivated Plants and Domestic Animals," p. 327 ff., the introduction of the citron into Europe is placed too late; for Herr in Zurich found citron seeds already in early Etruscan graves. In Egypt it was probably known early; and among the plants and fruits depicted by Thutmosis III, 18th Dynasty, at Karnak (Mariette XXX), one is probably our citron. Theophrastus's description, dating from the time of Alexander, of the Median or Persian apple IV, 4, 2 is well known. Virgil, Georgica III, 126, calls it "felix." — In any case the citron was already among the remedies proposed by Dioscorides (1st century A.D.). He calls it μηδικόν scil. μῆλον, κεδρόμηλον and in Latin κίτρια (citria) and assumes its general familiarity. His description leaves no doubt that the citron is meant. To be sure, he attributes to it far less healing power than to the onion. Taken with wine it is supposed to counteract poisons and act as a purgative; cooked, it is supposed to give the mouth pleasant breath, and it is most frequently used by women against loss of appetite and nausea (πρὸς τὴν κίσσαν). Finally, it is supposed to protect clothing from being eaten away when placed among them in the chest. That is all; whereas we see Dioscorides applying the onion in a manner that would by itself suffice to show that Egyptian therapeutics, and indeed perhaps a work similar to our Papyrus, was well known to him. LIII, 1 recommends the onion against sȳt °̣ᵢᵢᵢ, which seems to us to mean hemorrhoids. Fresh or green onion is to be placed in water in a new lame-jar, and this — it is the whole prescription — drunk for 4 days. Onion water is therefore what is prescribed, — and in Dioscorides, in the chapter dedicated to the onion (περὶ κρομμύων), this fruit is proposed as a remedy against hemorrhoids. Free of their skins and dipped in oil they can also serve, according to Dioscorides, in place of soap suppositories. Likewise, in our manuscript XXXIX, 9, 10, the dš °̣ᵢᵢ of the onion, cooked with oil (and honey), are to be used against complaints of the ro ab or os ventriculi, 4 times in the morning. näher zu bestimmen.

Entsprechend dem Gebrauche der Zwiebel bei Dioscorides ist
auch XXX, 19, wo für den Mastdarm 14 Zwiebeln mit süssem, nieder-
geschlagenen Bier verwandt werden sollen. Man thue, heisst es, dies in
ein dš ᵹ Gefäss, schliesse es ab gegen das Verderben, wende es
an wenn es den Niederschlag machte, gebrauche es in jeder Jahres-
zeit als Medicin und lasse davon täglich 1 Hin trinken. LXIX, 8—9,
wo ausser Zwiebeln auch die utyt ᵒ₁₁₁ der Zwiebel verordnet werden,
sind sie ein Mittel gegen das Grauwerden des Krebses; diese
utyt ᵒ aber dürfen wir wohl rohe Schalen übersetzen; ist doch die
Wurzel ut bekannt genug, die (wir weisen auf ᵒ) umwickeln, um-
hüllen bedeutet. Der aeg. Name der Oase ᵒ ᵸᵸᵸ ut ᵸᵸᵸ ist zwar
fälschlich mit dem kopt. oraʒe zusammengebracht worden, aber auch
das arabische wāḥ die Oase bedeutet ursprünglich das von der Wüste
umhüllte. XXVII, 20 soll āmē n tert ᵒ, d. i. das Innere oder
von der Schale befreite Fleisch der Zwiebel angewandt werden; ausser-
dem aber Pulver der (getrockneten) Zwiebel, und von der Meerzwiebel
bildet das Pulver einen Bestandtheil des Electuarium theriacale.
Bischoff, med. pharmac. Botanik. Erl. 1843. S. 703. XLIII, 16 soll
wieder gegen Verstopfung und »das Blutfressen?« am os ventriculi
entweder eine Paste von Sykomorenfeigen oder Zwiebeln von der
Oase genommen werden. Auf den Oasen der libyschen Wüste
werden noch heute vorzügliche Zwiebeln gezogen, und die Oasen-
zwiebeln scheinen im Alterthum, wie die von Ascalon, besonders
geschätzt worden zu sein. LXXXVI, 10 soll gegen übelen Geruch
am Leibe eines Mannes oder einer Frau eine Salbe von šḫm 𓌀
n tert ᵒ₁₁₁ d. s. gestossenen, gestampften Zwiebeln bereitet
werden, um den Leib damit einzureiben. Wir übersetzten die Krank-
heit ynš ᵹ »übeler Geruch« weil das kopt. ϣnoϥ foetor, colluvies,

Vielleicht hat man das χnδ ☽ aber auch fur Flechten (ἁlqoύς) zu halten, die Dioscorides mit Essig und Zwiebeln in der Sonne einzureiben räth. Uebrigens kann es sein, dass Dioscorides eher an LII, 20 denkt, wo geriebene Zwiebeln mit Honig und Bier oder Essig als Salbe gegen die Krätze δḥrt ☽ ≈ vorkommt. Die Verwendung der Zwiebel gegen Augenleiden stimmt gleichfalls mit Dioscorides überein, und wenn LXII, 1 [hieroglyphs] Saft der grünen oder frischen tert [hieroglyphs] für die »Eröffnung des Blickes« verschrieben wird, hat man wohl auch an Zwiebeln zu denken. Wir sahen sie schon gegen eine Krankheit der Augen vorschlagen; LXIII, 6—7 begegnet uns aber wieder fein zerriebene Zwiebel, die durch ein Tuch geseiht werden soll. Nachdem das so Gewonnene in Naturhonig (χpr tśf n áft [hieroglyphs]) geschlossen, soll es auf die erblindeten Augen gethan werden, und begegnen wir tert [hieroglyphs], d. s. Zwiebeln, auch sonst, z. B. LXI, 2 gegen Schmerzen in den Augen mit Honig und Öl, und gegen Kopfschmerzen, z. B. Schwindel im Kopfe, LXIV, 19, 21 und 22 (pulverisierte Zwiebel), so können wir wieder bei Dioscorides die Bestätigung unserer Bestimmung finden, da nach ihm — gerade wie in unserer Handschrift — Zwiebelsaft mit Honig gegen Kurzsichtigkeit, Hornhautgeschwulst (ἄγρεμον) Wölkchen oder Nubecula (νεφέλιον) und beim Beginn des Staares hilft. So kann denn tert [hieroglyphs] kaum etwas anderes sein als »Zwiebeln«, und dass es auch ☽ [hieroglyphs] determiniert wird, weist wahrscheinlich darauf hin, dass wir in ihm eine Frucht oder Substanz, der kräftiger Geruch eigen ist, zu erkennen haben. Zu den in Packeten importierten Drogen gehören die tert [hieroglyphs] nicht. Sie werden so häufig und in so grosser Quan­tität gebraucht, dass man sie für etwas leicht zu Beschaffendes, wahrscheinlich Einheimisches halten muss. Dagegen spricht keines­wegs, dass Zwiebeln von der Oase besonders verordnet werden; zieht man doch heute noch in Aegypten, das reich genug ist an Dattelarten, die von der Oase (Siwah) allen anderen vor, gilt doch in Berlin, dessen Handelsgärtnereien viele Zwiebeln ziehen, die

216                         Georg Ebers.                    [84

putredo etc. prompts us to place before our Recipe LXXXVI, 8 another one prescribing rubbing treatments against the χnδ ☽ in summer, where the unpleasant odor tends to be more pronounced. Perhaps the χnδ ☽ was also considered applicable to ringworm (ἁlqoύς), which Dioscorides advises rubbing in the sun with vinegar and onions. Moreover, it may be that Dioscorides is thinking rather of LII, 20, where grated onions with honey and beer or vinegar occur as an ointment against scabies δḥrt ☽ ≈. The use of the onion against eye ailments likewise agrees with Dioscorides, and when LXII, 1 [hieroglyphs] prescribes the juice of the green or fresh tert [hieroglyphs] for the "opening of sight," one must probably think of onions here too. We already saw them recommended against a disease of the eyes; LXIII, 6–7 we again encounter finely grated onion, which is to be strained through a cloth. After what is thus obtained has been enclosed in raw honey (χpr tśf n áft [hieroglyphs]), it is to be applied to blinded eyes, and we encounter tert [hieroglyphs], i.e. onions, elsewhere as well, e.g. LXI, 2 against pain in the eyes with honey and oil, and against headaches, e.g. dizziness in the head, LXIV, 19, 21 and 22 (powdered onion), so we can again find in Dioscorides confirmation of our identification, since according to him — just as in our manuscript — onion juice with honey helps against near-sightedness, corneal swelling (ἄγρεμον), cloudiness or Nubecula (νεφέλιον), and at the onset of cataracts. Thus tert [hieroglyphs] can hardly be anything other than "onions," and the fact that it is also determined by ☽ [hieroglyphs] probably indicates that we should recognize in it a fruit or substance with a strong odor. The tert [hieroglyphs] do not belong to the drugs imported in packages. They are used so frequently and in such large quantities that one must regard them as something easily obtainable, probably a domestic product. This is in no way contradicted by the fact that onions from the oasis are specifically prescribed; even today in Egypt, which is rich enough in date varieties, those from the oasis (Siwah) are preferred above all others, and even in Berlin, whose market gardens grow many onions,

"Lübbenauer" for the best. What external circumstances presently make impossible for us, others may undertake; we mean a careful examination of the images accompanied by inscriptions. Perhaps alongside a recognizable depiction of the onion one may still find its old name ſert ᵒ or ſert ᵒ₁₁₁; the Coptic ϩⲟλ, however, should probably be struck from the lexicon. Against this identification speaks also the fact that ſert ᵒ₁₁₁ is in any case feminine (ſert ᵒ₁₁₁ nt ⌣ an-s LXIII, 6, ſert ᵒ₁₁₁ net-t LXII, 4), while the authenticated form S. and B. ⲁ̄ⲕⲱλ is masculine. Such a change of grammatical gender would be a great rarity. On the other hand, the circumstance that the author of our manuscript attributes to the fragrant ſert ᵒ₁₁₁ fruits approximately the same effects as Dioscorides attributes to the onion seems to us to decide the question.

Briefly, though decisively, we wish to reject in conclusion Victor Loret's proposal to transcribe the hieratic group, which we render as ſert ᵒ₁₁₁, as ⌣ ſedt ᵒ, and then to equate ⌣ ſdt () ϩⲱⲣⲧ B., i.e., with the olive tree. The transcription that makes this identification possible is, however, entirely untenable, since the hieratic of Pap. Eb. shows ᵒ = t and ⌣ = r in a confusingly similar manner, but clearly distinguishes between ⌣ = r and ⌣ = d. In an isolated case a confusion of r and d might be possible, but one cannot entertain such a notion given the well over one hundred instances in which ſert ᵒ₁₁₁ is used with various determinatives in our manuscript. But it is also encountered elsewhere, and everywhere the ⌣ looks exactly as it does in Pap. Eb. Moreover, Herr Loret is unable to cite a single example in which ⌣ ſert ᵒ would be written. This notion is to be rejected entirely, both on external graphic grounds and on internal, substantive grounds. Fragment I of the London medical papyrus (I, 8), which mentions ᵒ₁₁₁ ᵒ₁₁₁ dbt ᵒ nt ſert ᵒ₁₁₁, was supposed to support H. Loret's second conjecture, that ſert ᵒ₁₁₁ is rather a mineral than a plant. But from which mineral could juice in abundant quantity be proposed

That a species of papyrus from the North should be found could have been expected from the outset, since the finest varieties of this plant thrived along the waterways of the Delta. The most excellent were those called Sebennytica, Tanitica, Saitica, etc., all of which were cultivated in the Delta. It is indeed questionable whether our equation geyt = ⲕⲓⲟⲟⲩⲧ is correct; for ⲕⲓⲟⲟⲩⲧ is attested only by a single source. Moreover, geyt is a feminine noun while ⲕⲓⲟⲟⲩⲧ is of the masculine gender. For this reason, a dagger (†) must also be placed after Cyperus.

28) ⲋⲟⲥ caprea, dorcas, dama, Arabian antelope. We need not be surprised to find animal excrement used even against eye ailments. Even in the Middle Ages, excrement was prescribed by physicians. The work known as the "Dreckäpotheke" (Filth Pharmacy) is well known enough, and Dioscorides likewise, in Book II, 98, in the chapter περὶ ἀποπάτων, lists mountain-goat dung among medications in addition to other kinds of dung. Boiled in vinegar or wine, it is to be applied against snakebite, ulcers, and erysipelas, and this last condition, "the rose," also occurs as venous thrombosis of the retina of the eye. The vulture's excrement mentioned at LVI, 15 is also known to Dioscorides as a remedy, l. l. p. 225; likewise that of various animals. Against eye ailments, there are also prescribed: LVII, 8 infant's stool, LIX, 1 bird droppings, LXIV, 1 fly excrement, LIX, 14 lizard's excrement.

30) kfeu', Coptic ⲕⲁϥ: truncus, ramus, caudex, etc. Yet it should be understood only as branches, because in XLVII, 2, the kfeu' of the ⲩⲉⲇⲧ plant are mentioned, and from LI, 16 it emerges that this plant grows along the ground, i.e., creeps along the earth. Such a plant cannot have a trunk. In XXXV, 9, the little balls of the kfeu' of flax (mḥe ⲙⲁϩⲓ == linum) are mentioned, and these can only be the capsules found at the tips of the small branches of the upward-branching hemp stalk. So kfeu' are boughs or branches, and perhaps under those of Upper Egypt one should see mastic branches; for the mastic pistachio (Pistacia Lentiscus) is said to occur in the northern Delta and other Mediterranean lands, but not in Upper Egypt. Its characteristic and closely related feature is precisely its reddish-brown younger branches. ādhyt can also be understood as marshland, and here perhaps one should think only of the branches of a marsh plant.

"That which has become from Stibium" is probably the more accurate translation, and by this one should understand Stibium oxide. 40) Was χpe von Ebenholz ist, wagen wir nicht sicher zu bestimmen. Es kommt übrigens auch von anderen Bäumen vor, wie vom Weihrauchbaum etc., doch nie so, dass es eine Handhabe böte. Es ist vorgeschlagen worden, es mit dem kopt. mma pudenda oder mit HcAni, φAne umbilicus, lumbus zusammenzubringen; doch was sind pudenda und der Nabel beim Auge? Dioscorides verordnet I, 129 Ebenholz fein pulverisiert, seine Drechsel- und Feilspähne, und es lässt sich vielleicht in dem kopt. S. B. msa scheeren wiederkennen. Das Abgeschorene, Geschnittene, oder wohl auch das Abgehobelte vom Ebenholz würde gut zu Dioscor. I, 129 passen.

41) Durchaus sicher bestimmt. Ebenholz kommt schon ausserordentlich früh vor. Im alten Reiche im Grabe des Ti »das Polieren« des Ruhebettes ⟹. Das Möbel ward schwarz gemalt und so, dass man es nur für Ebenholz halten kann. Von demselben Holze ward früh die Kopfstütze ⟹ gefertigt. Die Flotte der Hátšpsu brachte es aus Punt. Näheres bei E. Moldenke über die in altaegyptischen Texten erwähnten Bäume S. 93 ff. Hebr. Sing. הָבְנִים (Ges.) Plur. הָבְנִים. Diospyros Ebenum L. Bei Plinius hist. nat. 25, 41 als Mittel gegen die Augenleiden albugo und caligo. Das erstere ist die weisse Farbe und der weisse Fleck der Hornhaut = »λείωμα«. Nach Hirschberg S. 3 bedeutet albugineus auch das Kammerwasser, die Augenflüssigkeit (Galeno adscript. lib. d. ocul. p. 124). Dies würde für unser Recept stimmen. Das caligo, welches nach derselben Stelle des Plinius Ebenholz verwandt werden soll, ist Blödsichtigkeit im Allgemeinen. Nach Dioscorides I, 129 hat Ebenholz die Wirkung, die Pupillen von dem zu säubern, was sie verfinstert. Das sind doch die Ausflüsse, gegen die unser Recept sich richtet. In ganz fein pulverisiertem Zustand soll es am besten wirken. Als gute Zuthat für Augenmittel werden auch die Drechsel- oder Feilspähne des Ebenholzes in Wein von Chios aufgelöst bezeichnet. Statt des Weines kann man auch Wasser nehmen. Ebenholz soll auch in einem neuen irdenen Geschirr zu Kohle verbrannt, wie gebranntes Blei ausgewaschen und gegen ψωροφθαλμία und ξηροφθαλμία verwandt werden. It also occurs, by the way, from other trees, such as the frankincense tree etc., but never in such a way as to offer a handle for interpretation. It has been proposed to connect it with the Coptic mma pudenda or with HcAni, φAne umbilicus, lumbus; but what do pudenda and the navel have to do with the eye? Dioscorides prescribes in I, 129 finely powdered ebony, its lathe-shavings and filings, and one can perhaps recognize in the Coptic S. B. msa the word "to shave." The shavings, cuttings, or perhaps also the planed-off material from ebony would correspond well to Dioscorides I, 129.

41) Entirely certain in determination. Ebony appears extraordinarily early. In the Old Kingdom, in the tomb of Ti, "the polishing" of the bed ⟹. The piece of furniture was painted black and in such a way that one could take it only for ebony. The headrest ⟹ was early made from the same wood. The fleet of Hatshepsut brought it from Punt. In Pliny hist. nat. 25, 41 as a remedy against the eye conditions albugo and caligo. The former is the white color and the white spot on the cornea = »λείωμα«. The caligo, which according to the same passage in Pliny is to be treated with ebony, is dimness of sight in general. Pap. and likewise determined by [hieratic signs], is a fine anointing oil that is said to be used "on the right" among the hair preparations of our Pap. LXV, 16. 50) Stern connects the name of the plant [hieratic] mett (meté) with the Coptic метако, месало crocus and already correctly points to the μοδόδ in Dioscorides; however, this is chelidonium majus, not our crocus. What the papyrus otherwise says about this remedy will possibly lead the botanist to a certain trail. It is to be rubbed and pounded, LVIII, 20, against an eye disease with fresh water. Mentioned in connection with it are the prt [hieratic], that is the berries or the seed, as well as XXXIX, 20 [hieratic] ôâr o n mett [hieratic], that is the little stone or hard piece [a grain] (λλ lapis, calculus) of the same plant. There were various kinds of it, namely Southern mett [hieratic], Northern mett [hieratic], mett [hieratic] of the swamps (âdyt [hieratic] Pap. Eb. LXIX, 10 as well as in Berl. med. Pap. XIV, 2) of the land, or, as Brugsch [hieratic] translates, of the desert. In Pap. Eb. XLIII, 6, mett [hieratic] of the [hieratic], that is of the land and the north, are prescribed side by side. All of this fits quite well with the description of the χελεδόνιον μέγα in Diosc. II, 211, its Egyptian name μοδόδ (mett [hieratic]) and its use. The Romans were said to call it φάβιουμ (fabium), the Gauls Φύνα. The fruit is like that of the horned poppy, and the seed it contains is larger than a poppy seed. In it we can surely recognize the prt [hieratic], or the seeds, and the âr o, which would be equivalent to a single grain, of the mett [hieratic]. The juice mixed with honey, cooked on glowing coals in a bronze vessel, is said to be beneficial for sharp pains in the eyes, and was therefore also known to Diosc. as an eye remedy. With honey this mett [hieratic] is also prescribed in our papyrus, e.g. XLV, 4, mett [hieratic] of the north. Chelidonium majus still belongs today to the medicinal plants; in larger doses it acts as a poison, in smaller doses it stimulates all the secretory organs and promotes secretion in them. Bishop p. 173. That the Egyptians recognized this is evident from many recipes.

51) Entirely certain on account of the unambiguous meaning of [hieratic] and [hieratic]: heat, hot, to heat. Already the determinative [hieratic] of the flame would confirm it; but this is also supported by the combinations of the group. Perhaps the hieroglyphic teu [hieratic] corresponds to the Coptic χωφ, χοφχεφ meaning to burn. The transition of t into x is questionable.

a certain swelling on the eye "the barleycorn." For various reasons

stands in the singular does not contradict this in the least, since the same occurs with ailments

What leads Stern to translate it as "glaucoma" is unclear to us, and passages such as the Book of the Dead 26, 4 "he opened my blind eyes" place the meaning of šp beyond doubt. Among the variants collected by Naville in the Theban papyri, the Berlin Papyrus 2 has špwyn. Otherwise the Theban papyri have instead of šp — šdièu, šdntèu, šntu, šdnté and similar forms, which then refer to the eye as "broken" or "run out." "Dim-sightedness" might perhaps be substituted for blindness, and the cited passage of the Book of the Dead 26, 4 would then read: He opens my dim eye. The milk of decomposition or of going bad can mean nothing other than curdled sour or cheese-like milk, and so we maintain our view that in our group we see curdled or sour milk, especially since such might be more beneficial to the eye than flour-paste juice. Schrift, das, wie aus Z. 14 und 15 hervorgeht, bei der Mischung des anzuwendenden Mittels: Schildkrötengehirn mit Honig vorgelesen werden sollte. Ähnliche Stücke kommen LIX, 3—4 und 6 vor, und Plutarch, der in seiner Schrift über Isis und Osiris oft gut unterrichtet ist, erzählt Kap. 81, man habe Stellen aus den heiligen Schriften den Salbenbereitern vorgelesen, während sie die Droguen vermischten, welche das Räucherungsmittel Kyphi bildeten. Das hier angeführte Stück bezieht sich auf einen mythologischen Vorgang, und zwar wahrscheinlich auf den Kampf des Rā mit dem Set Typhon und seinen Gesellen. Eingeleitet wird der Streit durch ein Unwetter in der Nacht. Bei einem solchen denkt man sich den Set mit dem Horus oder, wie hier, mit dem Rā Harmachis im Streite. Es fällt dabei die heilige Säule, der Pfeiler auf dem das in Mumiengestalt aussculpierte Bild des Osiris angebracht ist, in's Wasser; d. h. der Osiris, für den der Kampf geführt wird, verschwindet in seinem Elemente, oder wie die Mythe sonst lehrt, in der Unterwelt. Nun schwingen die Gefährten des Rā die Stangen; denn mnāt ) bedeutet fraglos auch die Stütze oder den Pfahl und ist dasselbe wie das arabische nabbût, der starke und lange Holzstock in der Hand der Rhafire, der Führer etc., der zugleich als Stütze und Waffe dient und uns auch auf altaegyptischen Bildern häufig begegnet. Wir finden ihn in der Hand mancher Götter an Stelle des Scepters sowie in der der Matrosen, die bei den Jagden auf Krokodile etc. helfen, der Ortsvorsteher, Aufseher etc. Bei dem Kampfe gibt es ein gewaltiges Köpfen. Die Häupter fallen in's Wasser; doch der Gott weiss sie zu fangen (ân) wie Fische und sie den Verwundeten wieder aufzusetzen. Dies Abschneiden der Köpfe ist etwas sehr häufiges. Die Gegner der guten Götter kommen oft auch im Todtenbuche um die Köpfe, und das hsq tp sen, das Abschneiden ihrer Köpfe (Todtenb. 49, 3) ist eine dem Aegyptologen wohlbekannte Formel. Der Besucher der Königsgräber von Theben begegnet auch an den Grabwänden in den Scenen, welche das Leben in der Unterwelt darstellen, nicht wenigen auf dem Kopf oder den Füssen stehenden Gestalten mit abgeschnittenem Haupte. Aber auch das Wiederaufsetzen der Köpfe kommt mehrfach vor. Nach dem Kampfe des Set mit dem Horus schlägt der letztere der Isis, die sich des

This text, as can be gathered from lines 14 and 15, was to be read aloud during the preparation of the remedy to be applied: tortoise brain mixed with honey. Similar passages appear at LIX, 3–4 and 6, and Plutarch, who in his work on Isis and Osiris is often well informed, recounts in Chapter 81 that passages from the sacred writings were read aloud to the ointment makers while they mixed the drugs that formed the incense known as Kyphi. The passage cited here refers to a mythological event, most probably the battle of Rā against Set-Typhon and his companions. The conflict is introduced by a storm in the night. In such a storm, one imagines Set in battle with Horus or, as here, with Rā Harmachis. In the process, the sacred column — the pillar upon which the image of Osiris, carved in mummy form, is mounted — falls into the water; that is to say, Osiris, on whose behalf the battle is being fought, disappears into his element, or, as the myth teaches elsewhere, into the underworld. Now the companions of Rā swing their staffs; for mnāt undoubtedly also means the prop or the stake, and is the same as the Arabic nabbût, the strong and long wooden staff in the hand of the Rhafire, the leader, etc., which serves simultaneously as a support and a weapon and which we also frequently encounter on ancient Egyptian images. We find it in the hands of various gods in place of the scepter, as well as in the hands of sailors who assist in the hunting of crocodiles, etc., of local overseers, supervisors, etc. In the battle there is a tremendous beheading. The heads fall into the water; yet the god knows how to catch them (ân) like fish and to replace them on the wounded. This cutting off of heads is something very common. The enemies of the good gods also frequently lose their heads in the Book of the Dead, and hsq tp sen, the cutting off of their heads (Book of the Dead, 49, 3) is a formula well known to Egyptologists. The visitor to the royal tombs of Thebes also encounters on the tomb walls, in scenes depicting life in the underworld, no small number of figures standing on their heads or feet with their heads cut off. But the reattachment of the heads also occurs on several occasions. After the battle between Set and Horus, the latter strikes Isis, who had

242 Georg Ebers. [110

== Nothing speaks against Acacia nilotica except the circumstance that 'aś is described as growing on Libyan soil, in the oasis, and while the acacia thrives on the desert islands, the Cedar of Lebanon does not; we must investigate whether 'aś or the plant equated with it, prt śn, cannot mean something other than the Cedar of Lebanon or the acacia. We believe we should answer this question in the affirmative, and state here by way of anticipation that we consider prt śen to denote juniper berries and the tree of the same name, which the oasis inscription cited above calls 'aś from the western land or Libya, as one of the juniper, cypress, or thuya species, whose homeland was North Africa. Our reasons for this view are numerous and, we believe, decisive.

First of all, the Acacia nilotica can hardly be meant by the Libyan 'aś tree native to and growing on the oasis, because the latter (also called Mimosa nilotica or vera) occurs only from Senegal to Egypt (Leuxis' Botanik p. 367 § 274), whereas our prt śen, which is equated with it, is said to have been obtained from kpnė, a city that was certainly located in Phoenicia and is most likely the ancient Byblos (Gebal). Now the Nile acacia grows as little in Phoenicia as the Lebanon Cedar does in the oases; the Phoenician juniper (Juniperus phoenicea) is, however, a distinct variety of this plant, which according to Luxis (Botanik p. 104 f. § 623c) has red, very aromatic berries that are used throughout the Orient as well as in Greece in place of our black juniper berries, both in the household and in the pharmacy. It also yields the resinous juniper wood oil or cade oil (oleum cadinum). This still would not explain why the prt śn tree could be equated with the Libyan 'aś tree from the oasis; yet this circumstance too finds its explanation. The ancients counted the juniper among the cedars. In Dioscorides, for example, the Spanish juniper (Juniperus oxycedrus) is called κέδρος μικρα, and the precious Thuja (ὀντία) wood, which came from a tree that the Romans also called citrus, the Cedrus mauritanica and atlantica, was a North African tree. masern, its wood was so highly prized for the manufacture of luxury furniture and especially tabletops that, for example, Cicero paid nearly 100,000 marks for a single one. Plinius hist. nat. 5, 1, 13, 15, 16 and 30 has much to tell about this precious wood, which, despite its secondary name "citrus," certainly must not be taken for our citronwood. This species of thuja is by no means the tree named áš ꜣ or prt šn in the oasis inscription, but most probably the cypress or red-berried juniper, Juniperus phoenicea L., and the Greeks' μεγάλη ἄρκευθος, the great juniper, whose wood is burned and which looks very similar to the cypress. Already Dioscorides I, 103 found it ἐμφερὴς κυπαρίσσῳ, similar to cypress, and Sprengel showed in Dioscor. I, p. 387, that the κέδρος of the ancients is identical to juniperus phoenicea L. Theophrastus distinguishes ἄρκευθος from κέδρος, yet has the former, the juniper, also originating from Phoenicia. Amor is said to have carved his arrows from cypress wood, and it was also of special beauty, durability, and easily polished. Plutarch recommended it for its durability as a material on which all laws should be inscribed; many ships were built from it in the Mediterranean, and that it was especially suited for the making of beautiful temple doors is beyond question. The claim that all mummy coffins were made from it is false; however, we ourselves possess the nicely carved lid of a small box with a lion's head, which according to the determination of the botanist Langethal of Jena consists of cypress wood. Other Egyptian antiquities are of the same material, and like the cypress, juniperus phoenicea also grows on North African soil. The oasis inscription describes the áš ꜣ, which is said to be the same as prt šen, as that from the western land; if áš without further qualification were the same as mimosa vera or nilotica, one would nevertheless have to recognize in that from Libya a special species of acacia. Prof. Ascherson found wood remains from one such, as mentioned above, but the question remains whether the Egyptians were able to perceive the subtle differences that distinguish the mimosa vera of the oasis from that which grows along the Nile. Des Dr. Moldenke schon mehrfach erwähnte Strassburger Disser-
tation enthebt uns der Mühe, die Geschichte der Deutungen des Namens
'aš zu wiederholen. Chabas und de Horrack hatten schon früh die Ceder in ihm erkannt, und de Rouge's Übersetzung »Akazie« war bereits durch ihre guten Argumente zweifelhaft geworden. Brugsch und andere schlossen sich ihrer Erklärung gleichfalls an, bis die oben erwähnte Oaseninschrift Lepsius veranlasste 'aš für die Akazie zu erklären, weil die Libanonceder nicht in Libyen vorkomme, und 'aš auch bisweilen mit der Schote determinirt werde. Diese nun — wir wiederholen es — scheint ihm auf die Schoten tragende Akazie zu weisen, während sie wahrscheinlich blos auf den angenehmen Duft des sonst nur durch als angenehm riechend bezeichneten Baumes deutet. Brugsch schloss sich Lepsius in dem oben angeführten Aufsatze an, und so kam es, dass wir später ganz allgemein in Deutschland, Frankreich und England 'aš , , 'aš die Akazie übersetzen sehen. Nun verbietet — wir meinen es erwiesen zu haben — der blosse Umstand, dass nach der Oaseninschrift der libysche 'ašbaum dem prt sn gleichgesetzt und im Pap. Ebers prt sn aus Phönizien verordnet wird, 'aš für die Akazie zu halten, weil die einzige Art dieses Baumes, die hier gemeint sein könnte, Mimosa vera oder nilotica, in Phönizien nur als Fremdling vorkommt. Andere Gründe, die zum Theil schon von Chabas und de Horrack gefunden worden sind, und die Dr. Moldenke zusammenfasste, kämen dazu, uns in der Ansicht 'aš sei die Ceder und 'aš aus dem Westlande ein der Ceder verwandter Baum zu bestärken, und in

are to be weighed and measured, and Kusth found among the ancient Egyptian fruits in the Berlin Museum our "juniperus phoenicea."

It remains for us to investigate whether the tree, whose Libyan variety we recognized as juniperus phoenicea L. or the very similar cypress, is supposed to be equivalent to pr sn, and whether it in fact means cedar wherever it appears without further designation. We believe we should answer this question affirmatively and urge our colleagues to abandon the practice of translating 'aš as acacia.

Dr. Moldenke's Strasbourg dissertation, already mentioned several times, saves us the trouble of repeating the history of the interpretations of the name 'aš. Chabas and de Horrack had recognized the cedar in it at an early stage, and de Rougé's translation "acacia" had already been rendered doubtful by their good arguments. Brugsch and others likewise joined their interpretation, until the above-mentioned Oasis inscription led Lepsius to declare 'aš to mean acacia, because the Lebanon cedar does not occur in Libya, and 'aš is also sometimes determined with the pod. This now — we repeat it — seems to him to point to the pod-bearing acacia, whereas it probably refers merely to the pleasant fragrance of the tree, which is otherwise described only by as pleasant-smelling. Brugsch joined Lepsius in the essay cited above, and so it came about that we later see 'aš translated as acacia quite generally in Germany, France, and England. Now the mere circumstance — which we believe we have demonstrated — that according to the Oasis inscription the Libyan 'aš-tree is equated with prt sn, and in the Ebers Papyrus prt sn is prescribed from Phoenicia, forbids us from taking 'aš to mean acacia, because the only species of this tree that could be meant here, Mimosa vera or nilotica, occurs in Phoenicia only as a foreign plant. Additional reasons, some of which had already been found by Chabas and de Horrack and were summarized by Dr. Moldenke, would further strengthen the view that 'aš is the cedar and 'aš from the western land is a tree related to the cedar, and in

In recent times our friend J. Dümichen, who is particularly well versed in this matter, has also returned to the old and astute Chabas' original explanation. The very circumstance that the so frequently mentioned 'ash-wood is almost everywhere, where a more precise designation follows, described as genuine or as coming from abroad, prevents us from taking it for the acacia wood native to the Nile, of which counterfeit varieties are scarcely conceivable. With regard to cedar the situation was different. The genuine was probably that from Lebanon or from Asia — the one from the "Western Land" of the oasis inscription, the cypress or juniperus phoenicea, was probably the counterfeit variety. We resist repeating C. Piehl's⁶⁹) diligent compilation of objects that were customarily made from 'ash-wood, and of what was to be donated from them to the temples by the Pharaoh. The former, of which we noted a long list from various times and places, were mostly fine, adorned with inlays and partly of such a nature that they could scarcely have consisted of acacia wood. This is particularly hard to believe concerning the slender masts erected before the temple gates, for the production of which the moderately tall, rarely perfectly straight trunks of the mimosa nilotica would have been ill-suited, while the towering trunk of the cedar was ideally suited for such purposes. When the gates are described as "beautiful," they must ordinarily be of 'ash-wood. [hieroglyphic signs] his beautiful gates of 'ash-wood (Zeitschr. 1875, Pl. II. l. 35) recurs in numerous similar writings. The Palestinian oaks and 'ash [hieroglyphic signs] trees that reach the sky, from Pap. Anast. I, 19, 2, were already mentioned above. For the construction of ordinary Nile vessels acacia was used; yet De Horback has already shown that the ceremonial and festival ships consisted not of acacia but rather of 'ash or cedar wood. In support of his view he cites a passage from the Lateran obelisk in Rome, from which it emerges that Thutmosis III had the great festival barque of Amon of Thebes made from genuine 'ash-wood, which he had felled at the place Rṯẖ [hieroglyphic signs] in the land of Rṯẖ, (not instead of rôn) which by no means forms a part

Aegyptens, sondern nur das asiatische Land bezeichnet, aus welchem das χsbd (alt: χsbf) oder Lapis lazuli bezogen wurde, das so oft unter den Tributen der Asiaten genannt wird und von dem sich viele Gegenstände erhalten haben. In Vorderasien so weit die Aegypter kamen, gedieh die mimosa nilotica nicht, und kam sie dort auch als Fremdling vereinzelt und in weit weniger voll entwickelten Exemplaren vor als in der Heimat, wozu hätte man sie importieren sollen, da sie im Nilthal sehr viel häufiger und schöner gedieh. Unsere Akazie, die jetzt auch in Asien vorkommt, ist ein aus Amerika importierter Baum. In den Ptolemäertempeln ist häufig angegeben, dass die Thüren aus ꜥšḥolz bestanden, das oft «echt» genannt wird⁷⁰). Findet die Provenienz sich erwähnt, wird Aegypten, wo die Ceder vom Libanon garnicht, die Akazie aber um so besser fortkam, niemals genannt, dagegen aber stets eine oder die andere Landschaft, die man zwar nicht näher bestimmen kann⁷¹), die aber immer nur in Asien zu suchen ist.

Dazu haben wir ja in šndt (alt) ganz sicher die Nilakazie, mimosa nilotica, deren Namen sich im koptischen ϣоптє, ϣꜣнт und seinem Nachkömmling, dem arabischen «Sunt» recht wohl erhielt. Diese kam schon im alten Reiche als der Baum vor, von dem man, entsprechend der Beschreibung des Herodot (II, 90), die Lastschiffe in Aegypten baute. Als eigentlicher Charakterbaum des Nilthales wird er in den Nomenlisten in den verschiedenen Gauen 24 mal als heiliger Baum genannt, während in den nämlichen Listen der ꜥšbaum kein einziges mal vorkommt. Wäre ꜥš nur ein anderer Name für šndt gewesen, so hätte er an einer oder der anderen Stelle der Listen erwähnt werden müssen, zumal man keineswegs streng an einer bestimmten Schreibung des

Zu solcher kostbaren Auszierung wird das ꜥšholz auch anderwärts erlesen, und es muss schon darum eher das Cedern- als das in jeder Hinsicht geringere Akazienholz sein.

Egypt, but only the Asiatic land is designated, from which the χsbd (old: χsbf) or lapis lazuli was obtained, which is so often mentioned among the tributes of the Asiatics and from which many objects have been preserved. In the Near East, as far as the Egyptians went, the mimosa nilotica did not thrive, and it appeared there only sporadically as a foreign plant in far less fully developed specimens than in its homeland — why would one have imported it, since it thrived so much more frequently and beautifully in the Nile Valley? Our acacia, which now also occurs in Asia, is a tree imported from America. In the Ptolemaic temples it is frequently stated that the doors consisted of ꜥš-wood, which is often called "genuine." When the provenance is mentioned, Egypt — where the cedar from Lebanon does not grow at all but the acacia thrives all the more — is never named, but instead always one or another region which cannot be more precisely determined, but which is always to be sought only in Asia.

To this we may add that in šndt (older form) we have quite certainly the Nile acacia, mimosa nilotica, whose name was well preserved in the Coptic ϣоптє, ϣꜣнт and its descendant, the Arabic "Sunt." This appeared already in the Old Kingdom as the tree from which, according to the description of Herodotus (II, 90), the cargo ships in Egypt were built. As the characteristic tree of the Nile Valley it is named in the nome lists of the various nomes 24 times as a sacred tree, while in those same lists the ꜥš-tree does not appear a single time. Had ꜥš been merely another name for šndt, it would have had to be mentioned in one or another place in the lists, especially since one by no means strictly adhered to a particular spelling of the

in the Pap. Ebers regarded as the tree occurring in the form šndt. The consonants at the beginning of its second syllable we see written rather as d, (poorly) ȝ, and (archaic) t. But if such great license was permitted in the orthographic rendering of its name, it would presumably also have been permissible to call it by the name 'aš, if this had designated only the Nile acacia like šndt (Pap. Harris I šntô). It would be further remarkable if the garden enthusiast ʾinnâ, who lists the names and number of the trees he had planted and tended on his estate (there were 20 kinds), had forgotten the Nile acacia. Of the juniper, which he calls zt n šn the wood of the curl or curly-wood (p. 245 (113)), he possessed 3 specimens. 90 sycamores, 31 Persea? trees, 170 date palms, 120 doom palms, etc. flourished in his garden, and so the Nile acacia must also have stood there. We would like to identify the or pod-tree, of which he possessed 16 specimens, with it. The fact that a comparison of the texts from Dendera and Edfu yields the variant does not prevent us from this determination, which we intend to substantiate elsewhere. In the aforementioned Ptolemaic temples prt, i.e. seeds of the same, occur. The 'aš tree is described as a foreign tree that did not thrive in Egypt, and is also not mentioned in the tomb of Ânnâ.

The author of the Pap. Ebers prescribes from the 'aš tree the 'ad (fat or resin) for the head XLVIII, 12 and the glands of the neck LII, 14. The zp n 'aš are prescribed XLVI, 13–14 against the evil 'aéa illness in a remedy that the god Râ prepared for himself, and LXXVII, 21 against diseased toes; and they likely mean "filings" p. 225, (93). The wood of the 'aš tree, rubbed with milk, helps against scurf after it has fallen off; the ust or of the 'aš tree, i.e. the shavings obtained by sawing or filing its wood, are prescribed LXXVI, 6 against blood-blisters (nest of blood), LXXXIII, 1 in a

250 Georg Ebers. [118

complicierten Salbe zur Einreibung eines Gefässes (Nerv, Ader etc.), XCIII, 19 gegen prolapsus uteri verordnet. – Das ∂s (⌐ᵢ) LXXIV, 13 des ᾿ásbaumes wird wie das Holz desselben gegen Schorfe verwendet und bedeutet, dem koptischen zice hoch sein etc. und dem ursprünglichen Werthe der Wurzel ∂s entsprechend, sich erheben, die Erhebung und Spitze. Der so genannte Theil eines Baumes kann, als Medicament verordnet, schwerlich sein Gipfel sein, wahrscheinlich dagegen die Spitze der Zweige; denn an die Zapfen darf man kaum denken, weil ausser vom ᾿ásbaum auch von der Pflanze ↑⌐ rst ⌐ das ∂s verordnet wird, und rst ⌐ eine prägnant riechende Pflanze ist (XXI, 15), die kaum etwas anderes bedeuten kann als unser Calmus.

Überblicken wir diese Verwendung des ᾿ús ⌐ baumes, so müssen wir zunächst bemerken, dass das ᾿ád desselben wahrscheinlich jenes Cedernöl ist, womit schon die Alten Holz bestrichen, um es gegen Wurmfrass zu schützen und das von den Aegyptern zum Zweck der Balsamierung der Mumien fleissig benutzt ward. Das wissen wir durch die Alten (Herod. II, 87); Czermak fand aber auch bei der Untersuchung zweier prager Mumien, dass man das Siebbein der Nase des Leichnams zersprengt hatte, um durch dasselbe Cedernöl, das sich in getrocknetem Zustand vorfand, in den Schädel zu spritzen. Akazienöl hat sich nirgends in balsamierten Leichen gefunden. Was der Pharmaceur von der Mimosa vera oder nilotica benutzt, ist nur das Gummi und der Gummischleim (mucilago gummi Mimosae) sowie der succus acaciae verae, ein aus den unreifen Früchten bereiteter, tonisch adstringierender Extract, der aber nie und nimmer Akazienfett genannt werden konnte. Ebensowenig lassen sich Akazienpähne als Medizin denken. Ausser diesen Theilen oder Producten der Ceder begegnet uns auch das – hätt nt ᾿ás ⌐ oder Cedernöl (auf zahlreichen Opferlisten), das zu den hochgeschätzten Naturproducten gehörte, die man »Ausflüsse des Auges der Gottheit«, später sogar »das Auge des Horus« nannte und den Göttern darbrachte. Es blieben Altäre — die schönsten sahen wir im Museum zu Bulaq — mit den Vertiefungen erhalten, in welche man die Substanzen goss, deren Geruch den Nasen der Götter genehm war.
translation:
250 Georg Ebers. [118

complicated ointment prescribed for rubbing onto a vessel (nerve, vein, etc.), XCIII, 19, against prolapsus uteri. – The ∂s (⌐ᵢ) LXXIV, 13 of the ᾿ás tree is used like the wood of the same against scabs and means, corresponding to the Coptic zice "to be high," etc. and to the original value of the root ∂s, to rise up, the elevation and tip. The so-called part of a tree, when prescribed as a medicine, can hardly be its crown, but more likely the tips of the branches; for one can scarcely think of cones, since besides the ᾿ás tree, the ∂s is also prescribed from the plant ↑⌐ rst ⌐, and rst ⌐ is a strongly scented plant (XXI, 15), which can hardly mean anything other than our Calmus.

If we survey this use of the ᾿ús ⌐ tree, we must first note that the ᾿ád of the same is probably that cedar oil with which the ancients already coated wood to protect it against woodworm, and which was used diligently by the Egyptians for the purpose of embalming mummies. We know this through the ancients (Herod. II, 87); but Czermak also found, in the examination of two Prague mummies, that the ethmoid bone of the nose of the corpse had been broken open, in order to inject through it the cedar oil that was found there in a dried state into the skull. Acacia oil has been found nowhere in embalmed corpses. What the pharmacist uses from the Mimosa vera or nilotica is only the gum and the mucilage (mucilago gummi Mimosae) as well as the succus acaciae verae, an extract prepared from unripe fruits, tonically astringent, but which could never and can never be called acacia fat. Equally, acacia shavings cannot be considered as medicine. Besides these parts or products of the cedar, we also encounter the – hätt nt ᾿ás ⌐ or cedar oil (on numerous offering lists), which belonged to the highly valued natural products that were called "outflows of the eye of the Deity," later even "the Eye of Horus," and were presented to the gods. Altars have been preserved — the finest we saw in the museum at Bulaq — with the recesses in which the substances were poured, whose fragrance was pleasing to the noses of the gods.

419| Pap. Ebers. Die Maasse u. das Kapitel über die Augenkrankheiten. 251

Weil das Cederöl bei der Mumisierung der Leichen eine so grosse Rolle spielte, sollen es nach Dioscorides einige »das Leben der Todten« genannt haben, und man sagte ihm nach, dass es belebte Körper verderbe, verstorbene aber erhalte. Dennoch ward es als Medicament benutzt, und wir hören Dioscorides sagen, dass man es den Mitteln gegen Augenkrankheiten beigebe, da man durch Salbung damit die Schärfe des Gesichtssinnes stärke und die Leukome und vernarbten Wunden (οὐλάς) im Auge heile. Hier scheint Dioscorides, wie auch Sprengel vermutet, unter κέδρος nicht die Ceder vom Libanon zu verstehen, sondern juniperus phoenicea⁷²). Diese Wachholderart erkannten wir schon in dem 'aš ♀ des Westlandes, das auf der Oaseninschrift dem prt śn gleichgesetzt wird, — und so erklärt es sich, dass wir von der Libanonceder nichts, wohl aber an unserer Stelle prt śn gegen Augenleiden verordnet werden sehen.

Neben 'aš hat L. Stern auch sbt, sbt, sebt ○ für die Ceder erklärt und mit dem kopt. eige, cigi cedrus zusammengebracht; doch jedenfalls irrthümlich; denn statt dem γrn sbt das er 4 mal nennt, muss es überall heissen γt n ksbt. Der Umstand, dass ein Strich durch das Ende des hieratischen k ging, veranlasste ihn für zu halten, doch zeigt uns XX, 2 ganz deutlich »n ksbt«. Der Strich durch die Spitze des k ist der zu gehörende. sbt und γrn sind also zu streichen.

So haben wir denn in prt śn eine Wachholderart, wahrscheinlich juniperus phoenicea L. zu sehen. 'aš oder 'aš ist nicht die Nilakazie, mimosa vera oder nilotica, sondern die Ceder vom Libanon. 'aš des Westlandes ist gleich dem prt śn juniperus phoenicea⁷³) oder der dieser Pflanze ähnlichen Cypresse. Wenn Moldenke auch in prt ûan

translation:
419| Pap. Ebers. Measurements and the Chapter on Eye Diseases. 251

Because cedar oil played such a great role in the mummification of corpses, some people, according to Dioscorides, are said to have called it "the life of the dead," and it was alleged that it corrupted living bodies but preserved dead ones. Nevertheless it was used as a medicine, and we hear Dioscorides say that it was added to remedies against eye diseases, since by anointing with it one strengthens the sharpness of vision and heals leucomas and scarred wounds (οὐλάς) in the eye. Here Dioscorides seems, as Sprengel also suspects, to mean by κέδρος not the cedar of Lebanon but juniperus phoenicea⁷²). We already recognized this species of juniper in the 'aš of the western land, which is equated with prt śn in the oasis inscription — and this explains why we see nothing prescribed from the Lebanon cedar, but quite clearly find prt śn prescribed at our passage against eye ailments.

Alongside 'aš, L. Stern also explained sbt, sbt, sebt ○ as cedar and linked them with the Coptic eige, cigi cedrus; but this is in any case erroneous, for instead of γrn sbt, which he names 4 times, it must everywhere read γt n ksbt. The circumstance that a stroke passed through the end of the hieratic k led him to take it for, yet XX, 2 shows us quite clearly »n ksbt«. The stroke through the top of the k belongs to. sbt and γrn are therefore to be struck out.

Thus in prt śn we have a species of juniper to see, most probably juniperus phoenicea L. 'aš or 'aš is not the Nile acacia, mimosa vera or nilotica, but rather the cedar of Lebanon. 'aš of the western land is equivalent to prt śn juniperus phoenicea⁷³) or the cypress resembling this plant. When Moldenke also in prt ûan

78) P. 231 (99) note 50 on LVII, 12. According to Dioscorides, poultices with wine and the root of Chelidonium majus are also supposed to heal herpetic sores [ἑρπυγας]. Herpes, literally "the creeping thing" from ἕρπειν, also occurs on the eyes. Hirschberg mentions, for example, herpes corneae, where groups of water-clear blisters (up to a dozen and more) form under inflammatory manifestations, often together with herpes labialis and also with inflammation of the respiratory organs. Our symbol perhaps refers to the rim of the eyes and lips, which simultaneously show herpes, which is to be treated with Chelidonium majus. This is our common celandine, whose poisonous root, called goldwurz, is most richly provided with the yellow dye of this plant. It has nothing in common with crocus except that both appear early (the Chelidonium, true to its name, appears at the arrival of swallows) and yellow dyes are obtained from both remedies. In the case of Chelidonium, the root contains these most abundantly, as noted; in crocus, the stigmas. These are extracted with part of the style, dried, and come to market under the well-known name "saffron." In Diosc. I, 23, crocus is also counted among eye remedies and prescribed against erysipelas (rose) and flux of the eyes and ears (καὶ πρὸς ῥευματισμὸν ὀφθαλμῶν καὶ ὤτων). Here one should not think of our modern rheumatism. It has been difficult for us to choose between Chelidonium majus and crocus.
